IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
INHERENT/CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
SUO MOTO WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO(S). 8 OF 2025  
 
IN RE: 2 MILLION LIVES AT RISK, 
    CONTAMINATION IN JOJARI RIVER, 
    RAJASTHAN 
 
WITH 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 5517-5519 OF 2022 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 8748 OF 2022 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 9057-9058 OF 2022 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 9010-9011 OF 2022 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. The proceedings before this Court have, over 
time, brought to the fore several interrelated issues 
concerning the protection and restoration of the 
Jojari-Bandi-Luni River ecosystem, including 
pollution and discharge of untreated industrial 
effluents, encroachments upon riverbeds and 
floodplains, determination of the High Flood Line and 
ecological buffer zones, treatment and remediation of 
accumulated industrial wastewater, and the need for 

--- Page 19 ---
2 
 
effective institutional coordination. Having regard to 
the successive reports of the High-Level Ecosystem 
Oversight Committee 1, the Special Investigation 
Team, the compliance reports of the State of 
Rajasthan and the submissions of the respective 
parties, this Court, vide order dated 7th August, 2026, 
directed the constitution of an Integrated 
Coordination Group headed by the Chief Secretary, 
State of Rajasthan, and entrusted it with the task of 
formulating, in consultation with the Committee, a 
Comprehensive Resolution Plan setting out 
actionable measures, responsible authorities, 
measurable milestones, timelines and a monitoring 
mechanism. The Cou rt also issued directions 
concerning the scientific determination of the High 
Flood Line and ecological buffer zones, protection and 
restoration of the river system and remediation of the 
affected sites. 
2. Thereafter, vide order dated 24th August, 2026, 
this Court, inter alia , prescribed an interim and 
measurable area of protection pending scientific 
determination of the High Flood Line and ecological 
 
1 Hereinafter, being referred to as “Committee”. 

--- Page 20 ---
3 
 
buffer zones, clarified the respective roles of the 
Committee and the Integrated Coordination Group, 
and reiterated that the powers, functions and 
mandate entrusted to the Committee under the 
earlier orders would continue to operate in full force. 
Having regard to the interdisciplinary nature of the 
issues, the Court also entrusted the National Law 
University, Jodhpur with a project concerning 
environmental law and policy, institutional 
mechanisms, ecological restoration and the interests 
of affected commun ities. The Court further 
considered the issue relating to the accumulated 
wastewater at HRTS, Ambey Valley and, upon 
consideration of the proposal of the R ajasthan State 
Pollution Control Board2 and the recommendations 
of the Committee, permitted its treatment and the 
release and reuse of RO permeate subject to 
stipulated safeguards, with the RO reject to be dealt 
with through an approved scientific disposal 
mechanism. The matter was thereafter directed to be 
listed as part -heard on 22 nd September, 2026 for 
consideration of the Comprehensive Resolution Plan.

Status Report setting out the progress made in 
respect of the directions issued by this Court from 
time to time. The Committee has also placed on 
record its detailed comments on the  draft

Measures for Restoration and Protection of River

Enforcement Requiring Directions from th is Court, 
setting out the measures which, in its assessment, 
require urgent consideration and appropriate

4. When the matter was taken up on 22 nd 
September, 2026, a request for accommodation was 
made on behalf of the State of Rajasthan. The matter 
was, accordingly, directed to be listed on 29 th 
September, 2026. In the interregnum, the State of 
Rajasthan placed on record an additional Status 
Report, setting out its submissions in respect of, inter 
alia, the concerns relating to the amendment to the 
Guidelines dated 17 th September, 2026 issued by 
RSPCB for captive ETP-ZLD textile processing units; 

--- Page 22 ---
5 
 
the disposal of consent applications for captive ETP-
ZLD units; the closure of outlets and removal of 
concealed illegal pipelines; and the distance criteria 
of 100-500 metres from the High Flood Line and the 
boundaries of the rivers. 
5. At the hearing on 29 th September, 2026, Mr. 
S.V. Raju, learned Additional Solicitor General 
appearing for the State of Rajasthan, requested two 
weeks’ time to enable the State to convene a meeting 
with the Committee and deliberate upon the 
comments made by it on the Comprehensive 
Resolution Plan, particularly with regard to the 
concerns raised in relation to the extended timelines 
proposed for certain actionable points. It was 
submitted that the proposed deliberations would 
enable the State to address the concerns raised by 
the Committee and place before this Court a finalised 
Comprehensive Resolution Plan. 
6. Mr. Rishabh Sancheti, learned counsel 
appearing for the applicant, Jodhpur Pollution 
Control and Research Foundation, in I nterlocutory 
Application Nos. 299204  of 2026 (Application for 
Directions) and 299206  of 2026 (Application for 
Intervention), has drawn the attention of this Court 

--- Page 23 ---
6 
 
to the steps being undertaken for augmentation and 
upgradation of the existing treatment infrastructure 
serving the textile industrial units in Jodhpur. It has 
been submitted that the existing Common Effluent 
Treatment Plant (CETP), having an installed capacity 
of approximately 18.5 Million Litres per Day , is 
presently operating at a lower effective capacity owing 
to the characteristics of the effluent received, and 
that the applicant has undertaken a structured 
technical and commercial exercise for its upgradation 
and conversion into a Zero Liquid Dischar ge (ZLD) 
facility. The proposed system incorporates, inter alia, 
physico-chemical treatment, biological treatment, 
filtration, Dissolved Air Flotation (DAF), enhanced 
aeration, Ultrafiltration (UF) and Reverse Osmosis 
(RO) systems, together with Mechanical Vapour 
Recompression (MVR) and Agitated Thin Film Dryer 
(ATFD) for management of the RO reject, with the 
treated RO permeate proposed to be reused within 
the textile cluster. It was further submitted that the 
proposed ZLD configuration has been subjected to 
independent technical scrutiny by way of a Detailed 
Project Report undertaken by  Dr. Ajit Pratap Singh, 
Senior Professor and  Dean, Civil Engineering 

--- Page 24 ---
7 
 
Department, Birla Institute of Technology & Science, 
Pilani.  
7. Learned counsel has submitted that, as a 
concrete step towards implementation, the applicant 
has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding 
dated 14th September, 2026 with Spray Engineering 
Devices Ltd. for development of the proposed ZLD 
facility, with a phased implementation commencing 
with a 4 MLD demonstration plant and thereafter 
progressive augmentation. It has been submitted 
that the proposed arrangement is intended to ensure

before further capacity is commissioned. It was,

RSPCB has not received a positive response, 
notwithstanding the steps already undertaken by the

the existing treatment infrastructure. Learned 
counsel has also pointed out that the reuse of the RO 
permeate would require an adequate redistribution 
pipeline/network, which is presently not available, 
and has accordingly sought appropriate directions to 
the State of Rajasthan, RSPCB and RIICO to facilitate 
the necessary infrastructure and to process the 

--- Page 25 ---
8 
 
requisite permissions in a time -bound manner, 
subject to compliance with all applicable 
environmental and statutory requirements. 
8. Having regard to the request made on behalf of 
the State, we deem it appropriate to afford an 
opportunity to the State to deliberate upon the 
concerns raised by the Committee and to place before 
the Court a concrete Comprehensive Resolution Plan. 
At the same time, the material placed before us, 
particularly the latest report of the Committee, 
indicates that the issues highlighted therein are not 
merely matters of administrative sequencing. They 
concern continuing sources of pollution, deficiencies 
in pollution-control infrastructure, enforcement gaps 
and impediments to the restoration and protection of 
the Luni river system. The Committee has, on the 
basis of its inspections and the material placed before 
it, identified several measures which, in ou r 
considered view, require to be addressed in a 
coordinated and time-bound manner. 
9. The first concern relates to the continued 
existence of identified illegal/unauthorized discharge 
points and unauthorised conduits, pipelines, bypass 
arrangements, manholes and chambers. The 

--- Page 26 ---
9 
 
Committee has noted that, in respect of several such 
mechanisms, the necessary investigation, mapping 
and evidentiary exercise has already been completed 
and clearance has been issued by the Special 
Investigation Team  paving the way for 
removal/dismantling of the illegal conveyance 
infrastructure. In such cases, the Committee has 
emphasised that completion of the wider survey for 
detection of concealed pipelines cannot be made a 
pre-condition for taking action against mechanisms 
which have already been identified, mapped and 
cleared for removal . Such illegal/unauthorized 
discharge points are required to be sealed or 
intercepted forthwith and the unauthorised, unused 
or abandoned pipelines and conduits removed, while 
the remaining survey proceeds simultaneously on an 
accelerated basis. 
10. The Committee has further emphasised the 
need for the aforesaid exercise to be accompanied by 
joint physical verification and district -wise Action 
Taken Reports. The object is to ensure that the action 
reported by the concerned authorities is subjected to 
physical verification and that the removal of 
unauthorised conduits and interception of discharge 

--- Page 27 ---
10 
 
points is not treated as complete merely on the basis 
of administrative correspondence. The Committee 
has, therefore, stressed upon a mechanism which 
permits verification of the action taken on the ground 
and its periodic reporting. 
11. Another concern relates to the continued 
establishment and operation of polluting and Red 
Category industries upon agricultural and residential 
lands. The Committee has highlighted instances 
where trenches, channels, deep pits, open effluent 
ponds and drainage net works have been created for 
disposal of large quantities of untreated industrial 
effluent directly upon agricultural fields. Such 
practices result in direct contact between untreated 
effluent and the soil and create a potential pathway 
for degradation of s oil and contamination of 
subsurface and groundwater, apart from the 
possibility of pollutants reaching adjoining drains, 
watercourses and, ultimately, the river system. 
12. The Committee has also noted that enforcement 
against such illegal industrial activity has 
substantially remained complaint -driven and 
reactive. Closure or dismantling of an individual unit, 
by itself, does not address the possibility of the 

--- Page 28 ---
11 
 
activity being re -established at the same or another 
location. The Committee has accordingly emphasised 
the need for a permanent, proactive and district-wise 
mechanism for detection and eradication of such 
activity, extending beyond notified industrial are as 
and involving the RSPCB, District Administration, 
Police/SIT, Revenue, Transport, local bodies and 
other concerned agencies. Such mechanism, as 
suggested by the Committee, would require identified 
nodal officers, recurring field surveillance and fixed 
timelines for action and follow-up. 
13. The Committee has further emphasised that 
enforcement in respect of an illegal industrial unit 
cannot end with closure of the premises. Every such 
detection, according to the Committee, ought to 
trigger investigation of the complete financial, job -
work, ra w-material, transport and beneficiary 
network sustaining such activity, including any 
authorised industry outsourcing work to such unit  
and should be followed by prosecution of the persons 
responsible under the extant statutes . 
Simultaneously, appropriate land -use and revenue 
proceedings, removal or lawful seizure of machinery, 
restoration of the affected land and prosecution are 

--- Page 29 ---
12 
 
required to be pursued. The Committee has also 
highlighted the need for unit -wise assessment, 
imposition and actual recovery of Environmental 
Compensation for the entire period of violation, with 
disclosure of the amount assessed, recovered and 
outstanding and the coercive measures undertaken 
for recovery. 
14. The Committee has drawn attention to the 
continuing deficit in pollution-control and treatment 
infrastructure. Proposals relating to augmentation of 
existing Common Effluent Treatment Plants (CETPs), 
conversion or upgradation to Zero Liquid Discharge 
(ZLD), establishment of new C ommon Effluent 
Treatment Plants and augmentation of individual  
Effluent Treatment Plants (ETPs) continue to remain 
at different stages before the concerned authorities. 
The Committee has observed that such pendency has 
a direct bearing upon the availability of adequate 
treatment capacity and, consequently, upon the risk 
of untreated or inadequately treated effluent entering 
drains, groundwater and the river system. It has, 
therefore, emphasised that such proposals be 
processed and decided within fixed timelines and has 
recommended a permanent single -window nodal 

--- Page 30 ---
13 
 
mechanism enabling their simultaneous technical, 
financial and statutory processing, with defined 
timelines, identified responsible officers and periodic 
monitoring. 
15. In the same context, the Committee has called 
for reconsideration of the existing State financial 
assistance and funding framework for pollution -
control infrastructure, so that financial constraints 
faced by Special Purpose Vehicles or industrial 
associations do not indefinitely delay the 
establishment or augmentation of essential CETP 
and ETP capacity, while preserving appropriate 
industry contribution in accordance with the Polluter 
Pays Principle. The Committee has also specifically 
identified the already sanctioned 7 MLD CETP (ZLD) 
at RIICO Industrial Area, Pali, Phase-I and II, and has 
recommended its immediate execution on a 
compressed, milestone -based schedule covering 
tendering, award, construction, commissioning and 
stabilisation. 
16. The Committee has, additionally, emphasised 
the need for strict implementation of the machinery-
based wastewater regime. It has recommended unit-
wise physical verification and actual removal of 

--- Page 31 ---
14 
 
machinery which exceeds the permissible 
wastewater-generating capacity. Mere sealing of such 
machinery, in its view, cannot constitute final 
compliance where the machinery remains capable of 
reactivation or misuse. The Committee has 
accordingly emphasised the necessity of 
photographic and geo -tagged verification and 
corresponding updating of the consent capacity so as 
to ensure that the machinery-based regime operates 
effectively on the ground. 
17. The Committee has also brought to the notice of 
this Court the concerns arising from  illegal 
Bajari/sand mining and the resultant devastation of 
the riverbed. It has noted that excessive, 
indiscriminate or unscientific mining may alter 
riverbed levels, create pits, disturb sediment 
movement, affect riverbanks and groundwater 
interaction and result in temporary roads, stockpiles 
and other impedi ments to the natural flow of the 
river. The Committee has accordingly sought 
complete information regarding permitted and illegal 
mining areas, leases, permitted quantities, 
replenishment position, mining depth and 
restoration obligations, so that the impa ct of such 

--- Page 32 ---
15 
 
activity and the applicable regulatory safeguards may 
be assessed on a river -wise and stretch -wise basis. 
We are constrained to note that, despite a reminder 
issued by the Committee, the requisite information 
has not been furnished by the concerned authorities. 
The failure to furnish the information sought by the 
Committee, particularly when the same is necess ary 
for a river -wise and stretch -wise assessment of the 
impact of mining and the corresponding restoration 
obligations, is a matter of serious concern.  
18. The Committee has, in the same context, drawn 
attention to instances where bridges, roads and 
associated structures, by reason of their design or 
construction, obstruct or are capable of obstructing 
the natural flow of the river and thereby operate as 
unintended or unauthorised anicuts or check-dams. 
Deficiencies such as inadequate waterway openings, 
absence of sufficient pipes or culverts and debris left 
within the riverbed have been noticed. The 
Committee has accordingly called for a 
comprehensive technical survey of bridges and road 
crossings across the Luni, Jojari and Bandi river 
systems and their tributaries, identification of 
structures impeding natural flow, location -wise 

--- Page 33 ---
16 
 
rectification, removal of artificial obstructions and 
appropriate safeguards for future constructions. 
19. Finally, the Committee has placed before the 
Court the position concerning HRTS, Ambey Valley, 
and the need for continued monitoring and time -
bound completion of the remediation exercise. The 
Committee has taken note of the progress made 
pursuant to the mechanism approved by this Court, 
under which the accumulated wastewater is to be 
conveyed to CETP, Balotra for treatment, with reuse 
of the RO permeate, subject to stipulated safeguards, 
including supervision by the RSPCB, daily testing, 
flow-meter based accounting and weekly reporting. 
The Committee has emphasised that the exercise 
must proceed continuously and on an accelerated 
basis until the accumulated wastewater is completely 
treated and disposed of, the hazardous sludge is 
scientifically removed, the redundant storage 
structures are dismantled and the affected land is 
restored. 
20. The aforesaid concerns, taken together, 
demonstrate that the restoration of the entire river 
ecosystem requires action at multiple levels , 
immediate interception of identified sources of 

--- Page 34 ---
17 
 
pollution, effective enforcement against illegal 
industrial activity, augmentation of treatment 
infrastructure, prevention of recurrence through 
coordinated surveillance, restoration of the riverbed 
and natural flow, regulation of mining activity and 
completion of the remediation of identified 
contaminated sites. While we acknowledge that 
certain enforcement and remedial measures have 
been undertaken by the authorities in pursuance of 
the directions issued by this Court  and the 
Committee. We are nevertheless constrained to note 
with concern that much remains to be done and that 
several of the issues identified by the Committee 
continue to suffer from lack of  concerted and time -
bound action. 
21. It is important to observe that the aforesaid 
concerns are not being raised for the first time. The 
issues relating to the existence and operation of 
illegal conduits and concealed pipelines, 
establishment of industrial units upon agricultural 
and residential lands, unauthorised change of land 
use, augmentation and effective utilisation of 
treatment infrastructure, as also the imperative need 
to restore and maintain the natural flow of the river, 

--- Page 35 ---
18 
 
have been brought to the notice of this Court time 
and again over the course of the last one year. This 
Court has, from time to time, issued specific 
directions with a view to securing remedial action and 
ensuring that these concerns are addressed in a 
sustained and effective manner. Yet, notwithstanding 
the passage of time and the repeated directions  
issued by this Court, it appears that the State and its 
functionaries continue to adopt a largely reactive 
approach, responding to instances as and when they 
are brought to its notice, rather than putting in place 
a proactive and preventive mechanism capable of 
addressing the problem in its entirety and preventing 
its recurrence. 
22. There is, in our view, a fundamental disbalance 
between the existing treatment infrastructure and 
the quantity of wastewater requiring treatment, 
which itself calls for urgent augmentation and 
efficient utilisation of the available infrastructure. It 
is, t herefore, a matter of concern that, on the one 
hand, the existing treatment infrastructure remains 
inadequate to meet the requirement, while, on the 
other hand, impediments appear to be placed in the 
way of industries which are willing to establish and 

--- Page 36 ---
19 
 
operate captive ETPs designed to achieve Zero Liquid 
Discharge. The Guidelines issued by the RSPCB on 
17th September, 2026, concerning the establishment 
of captive ETPs, prima facie , contain a number of 
highly technical, frivolous and onerous requirements 
which may have the effect of discouraging industries 
from undertaking the very measures necessary for 
the treatment and proper management of their 
effluents. The regulatory framework must facilitate, 
and not disincentivise, the cr eation of additional 
treatment capacity, while at the same time ensuring 
that such facilities conform to the requisite 
environmental standards. 
23. The establishment and continued operation of 
industrial areas in close proximity to the river 
ecosystem has, over the years, placed a severe 
burden upon the riverine environment. The 
cumulative discharge of untreated or inadequately 
treated effluents, unau thorised conduits, alteration 
of natural drainage patterns and associated 
industrial activities has consequences extending 
beyond the river itself, affecting the quality of soil and 
groundwater and, consequently, the health and well-
being of human populati ons, livestock and other 

--- Page 37 ---
20 
 
living organisms dependent upon the river 
ecosystem. The degradation of a river system of this 
nature cannot be viewed merely as an issue of 
regulatory non -compliance by individual industrial 
units. It raises a larger question as to the suitability 
of the location and spatial distribution of industrial 
activity in relation to the ecological carrying capacity 
of the riverine system.  
24. In these circumstances, it would be appropriate 
for the State to undertake a comprehensive 
assessment of the feasibility of relocating such 
industrial areas  having polluting industries , 
particularly those situated in close proximity to the 
river and its tributaries, to suitable locations where 
their environmental impact can be effectively 
contained and adequate treatment and disposal 
infrastructure can be ensured. Such an exercise may 
take into account the ecological sensitivity of the 
area, the carrying capacity of the river system, the 
availability of land and common treatment 
infrastructure, the feasibility of achieving Zero Liquid 
Discharge or other prescribed standards, the long -
term interests of the affected communities , and the 
financial viability of such relocation . The object 

--- Page 38 ---
21 
 
should be to evolve a sustainable spatial framework 
for industrial activity so that the restoration of the 
river ecosystem is not continually undermined by the 
continued concentration of polluting activities in its 
immediate vicinity. 
25. The material placed before us, when considered 
cumulatively, leaves little doubt that the difficulties 
confronting the Jojari -Bandi-Luni River ecosystem 
are not attributable to any isolated instance of non -
compliance. They arise from a combination of 
inadequate treatment capacity, continued operation 
of unauthorised industrial activity, ineffective control 
over land use and discharge mechanisms, 
insufficient surveillance and enforcement, and 
interventions which interfere with the natural course 
and flow of the river. The recurring nature of these 
concerns, despite the directions issued by this Court 
from time to time, demonstrates that a purely 
incident-based response is inadequate. There is, 
therefore, a dire need for a fundamental change in 
the manner in which the bureaucracy approaches 
these issues. The State machinery must shed its 
traditional reactive posture, move away from a 
practice of responding only after violations are 

--- Page 39 ---
22 
 
brought to its notice, and bring about an internal 
reorientation in its functioning so as to anticipate 
environmental risks, act proactively and ensure 
continuous coordination amongst the concerned 
authorities. 
26. We are conscious that the State and its agencies 
have undertaken several measures pursuant to the 
directions issued by this Court. At the same time, the 
material placed before us indicates that several of the 
concerns continue to persist and require focuse d 
attention. It is in this background, and having regard 
to the concerns highlighted before us, as also those 
repeatedly brought to the notice of this Court, that 
we are of the view that certain further directions have 
become necessary to ensure that these concerns are 
addressed in a coordinated, effective and time-bound 
manner. 
27. In view of the aforesaid discussion and the 
concerns noticed hereinabove, we feel that certain 
immediate and specific directions are necessary to 
address the issues brought to the notice of this Court 
and to ensure coordinated and time-bound action by 
the concerned authorities, which are as follows: - 

--- Page 40 ---
23 
 
A. The State of Rajasthan and its concerned 
authorities/officials shall ensure that all 
illegal/unauthorized discharge points, bypass 
arrangements, manholes, chambers, pipelines and 
conduits which have already been identified, 
mapped and cleared by the S pecial Investigation 
Team are sealed/intercepted or dismantled 
forthwith. Such action shall not be deferred or 
made contingent upon completion of the wider 
survey, even if the survey is presently underway, 
the identified points shall be acted upon 
immediately. The concerned officials shall 
thereafter undertake physical verification of the 
action so taken and submit an Action Taken 
Report to the Committee on a fortnightly ba sis, 
indicating the location, nature of the action 
undertaken and the present status of each 
identified point. 
B. The State of Rajasthan shall forthwith take 
effective and comprehensive  enforcement action 
against industrial units operating illegally upon 
agricultural or residential land. Every detection of 
such an illegal industrial unit shall trigger, apart 
from action against the unit itself, an investigation 

--- Page 41 ---
24 
 
into the entire financial, job -work, raw-material, 
transport and beneficiary network sustaining such 
activity, including any authorised industrial unit 
found to be outsourcing work to such illegal unit. 
Simultaneously, the concerned authorities shall 
initiate appropriate land -use and revenue 
proceedings against the landowner/occupier, 
removal or seizure of machinery, restoration of the 
affected land and prosecution of the persons 
responsible, strictly in accordance with law. 
C. The State of Rajasthan shall establish a 
permanent, district -wise and coordinated 
enforcement mechanism involving the RSPCB, 
District Administration, Police, Revenue, 
Transport, local bodies and other concerned 
agencies. The mechanism shall provide for 
identified nodal officers, regular and recurring field 
surveillance, inter-departmental coordination and 
clearly defined procedure for detection,  
enforcement action, follow-up and reporting, so as 
to ensure that instances of illegal industrial 
activity are identified and acted upon promptly. 
D. The State of Rajasthan and the concerned 
authorities shall strengthen and intensify 

--- Page 42 ---
25 
 
surveillance of notified industrial areas and the 
adjoining agricultural and residential areas, with 
particular attention to areas vulnerable to the 
establishment or relocation of unauthorised 
industrial units. Such surveillance shall be 
undertaken on a continuing basis so as to ensure 
that polluting industrial activities do not merely 
shift beyond the existing regulatory perimeter or 
re-emerge at other locations. 
E. The RSPCB shall initiate proceedings for 
assessment, imposition and actual recovery of 
Environmental Compensation for the entire period 
of violation from the concerned industrial units 
and other persons/entities found responsible or to 
have benefited from such violations. The RSPCB 
shall place before the Committee a statement 
indicating the Environmental Compensation 
assessed, the amount actually recovered and the 
amount, if any, remaining outstanding. 
F. The Chief Secretary, State of Rajasthan shall 
ensure that all pending proposals relating to 
augmentation of existing CETPs, conversion or 
upgradation to ZLD, establishment of new CETPs 
and augmentation of individual ETPs are 

--- Page 43 ---
26 
 
processed and decided within fixed and 
compressed timelines. For this purpose, the State 
shall establish a single -window or designated 
nodal mechanism to facilitate simultaneous 
technical, financial and statutory processing of 
such proposals, with identified responsible 
officers, prescribed timelines for  each stage and 
periodic monitoring of the progress. The status of 
each such proposal, including the stage at which 
it is pending and the reasons for any delay, shall 
be placed before the Committee on a periodic 
basis. 
G. The RSPCB shall  forthwith, in consultation with 
the Committee, undertake a review of the 
Guidelines dated 17th September, 2026 concerning 
captive ETPs and make such amendments as may 
be suggested by the Committee  to remove 
avoidable bottlenecks and unreasonable technical 
requirements which may have the effect of 
disincentivising industries from establishing 
captive ETPs, while ensuring compliance with all 
requisite environmental standards. 
H. The State of Rajasthan and the concerned 
authorities shall forthwith implement the 

--- Page 44 ---
27 
 
machinery-based wastewater regime in its true 
letter and spirit. We may note that similar 
directions had earlier been issued by this Court 
vide order dated 18 th March, 2026. However, the 
same have not been complied with in their 
intended form till date. The concerned authorities 
shall, therefore, undertake unit -wise physical 
verification of the machinery installed and the 
corresponding wastewater -generating capacity, 
and ensure removal or seizure of machinery found 
to be in excess of the permissible capacity, 
wherever required. The compliance shall be duly 
documented and verified so as to ensure that the 
regime is effectively implemented on the ground 
and is not rendered illusor y by subsequent 
reactivation or misuse of the machinery. 
I. The State of Rajasthan and the concerned 
authorities shall ensure immediate execution of 
the sanctioned 7 MLD CETP (ZLD) at RIICO 
Industrial Area, Pali, Phase-I and II. The execution 
shall proceed on a compressed, milestone -based 
timeline, covering tenderi ng, award of work, 
construction, commissioning and stabilisation, 
without avoidable administrative delay. 

--- Page 45 ---
28 
 
J. The State and the concerned authorities shall take 
immediate and effective enforcement action 
against all illegal and unauthorised Bajari/sand 
mining activities which have an adverse impact 
upon the riverbed, riverbanks or the natural flow 
and ecology of the river system. The complete 
information sought by the Committee, including 
details of permitted and illegal mining areas, 
leases, permitted quantities, replenishment, 
mining depth and restoration obligations, shall be 
furnished to the Committee forthwith and, in any 
event, on or before 15 th October, 2026, so as to 
enable a proper river -wise and stretch -wise 
assessment of the impact of such mining and the 
measures required for restoration and protection.  
The Chief Secretary, State of Rajasthan, shall 
ensure that the aforesaid information is placed 
before the Committee, duly supported by affidavits 
of the Secretaries of the Department of Mines and 
Geology and the Department of Water Resources. 
K. The State of Rajasthan and the concerned 
authorities/officials shall undertake a 
comprehensive technical survey of all bridges and 
road crossings across the Luni, Jojari and Bandi 

--- Page 46 ---
29 
 
river systems and their tributaries, identify 
structures which impede or are capable of 
impeding the natural flow of the rivers, undertake 
location-wise rectification and removal of artificial 
obstructions, and put in place appropriate 
safeguards to ensure that future construction does 
not interfere with the natural flow of the river 
system. 
L. The State and the concerned authorities shall 
ensure continued monitoring and time -bound 
completion of the remediation exercise at HRTS, 
Ambey Valley, in strict compliance with the 
safeguards stipulated by this Court vide order 
dated 24 th August, 2026. The entire exercise, 
including treatment and disposal of the 
accumulated wastewater, scientific removal of 
hazardous sludge, dismantling of redundant 
storage structures and restoration of the affected 
land, shall be taken to its logical concl usion. The 
concerned officials of the State shall carry out 
physical verification and submit Action Taken 
Report to the Committee on a fortnightly basis. 
M. The applicant, Jodhpur Pollution Control and 
Research Foundation, in Interlocutory Application 

--- Page 47 ---
30 
 
Nos. 299204 of 2026 (Application for Directions) 
and 299206 of 2026 (Application for Intervention), 
shall be at liberty to place its proposed project, 
together with the requisite technical material, 
before the Committee for its consideration. The 
Committee shall examine the proposal in the 
context of the concerns relating to augmentation 
of treatment inf rastructure and, upon such 
consideration, place its recommendations before 
this Court in its next report. 
N. The Integrated Coordination Group shall convene 
a meeting with the Committee at the earliest to 
consider the draft Comprehensive Resolution Plan 
in its entirety. Upon such consultation, the State 
shall finalise the Comprehensive Resolution Plan 
after duly considering and addressing the 
comments, observations and concerns of the 
Committee. The finalised Plan shall thereafter be 
placed before this Court with an advance copy to 
the Committee and shall clearly set out the 
measures proposed to be undertaken, the 
timelines for their implementation, the authorities 
responsible for their execution and measurable 
milestones for assessing progress. 

--- Page 48 ---
31 
 
O. The Integrated Coordination Group shall, while 
finalising the Comprehensive Resolution Plan, 
specifically incorporate therein the concerns and 
issues highlighted in the present order, so that the 
Plan comprehensively addresses the directions 
and observatio ns of this Court and provides for 
appropriate measures, timelines and institutional 
responsibility for their implementation. 
P. The State of Rajasthan shall undertake a 
comprehensive assessment of the feasibility of 
relocating industrial areas situated in close 
proximity to the Luni, Jojari and Bandi river 
systems and their tributaries, particularly where 
their continued operation poses a significant 
environmental burden upon the river ecosystem. 
The assessment shall take into consideration the 
ecological sensitivity and carrying capacity of the 
river system, availability of suitable land and 
common treatment infrastructure, feasibi lity of 
achieving Z ero Liquid Discharge or other 
prescribed environmental standards, and the long-
term interests of the affected communities. The 
State shall place the outcome of such assessment, 
along with its recommendations and a proposed 

--- Page 49 ---
32 
 
course of action, before the Committee for its 
consideration and recommendations to this Court. 
28. The Registry shall forward a copy of this order 
to Hon’ble Mr. Justice Sangeet Lodha, Judge (Retd.), 
High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan on his email 
address: j.sangeetlodha@gmail.com, as well as to Mr.

SLP (C) No. 5582/2023
O R D E R
Heard Mr. Ranjit Kumar, learned Senior Counsel, appearing on
behalf of respondent No. 82, Navi General Insurance Limited submits
that he has filed an affidavit in terms of the previous order.
2. Filing of the affidavit was necessitated in the background of
the fact that on 6th April 2026, this Court had issued notice to
the  said  respondent,  but  on  26th  May  2026,  there  was  no
representation and the Court had ordered that all the respondents
who had not entered appearance, the CMDs of those companies shall
remain personally present on the next date, which was indicated as
30th July 2026. However, when the matter was taken up on 17th
August 2026, despite it being a fact that till 26th May 2026, there
had been no appearance on behalf of respondent No. 82, as per the
order, he had to be physically present before the Court. That not
being done, the Court on 17th August 2026 directed the respondent
No. 82 along with respondents No. 45, 64, 77, 79, 89, 93, 94, 95,
98, 100, 102 and 103 to appear before this Court to file their
personally affirmed affidavit.
3. Today, in the affidavit filed, it has been stated that the
notice pursuant to the order of this Court dated 6th April 2026 was
received in the institution on 18th April 2026, but was somehow not
brought to the notice of the officers and was never processed, for
which  certain  persons  who  were  responsible  have  also  been
suspended.
4. At this juncture, when the Court wanted to know the current
status of the action against such officials who are set to be under

--- Page 59 ---
10
SLP (C) No. 5582/2023
suspension, the answer by the Managing Director himself is that it
was a bona fide error on their part.
5. We are shocked at this response by the Managing Director that
without even issuing any notice to the person concerned, he himself
has assumed that it was a bona fide error. 
6. We note that apology has been tendered in the affidavit but we
outright reject the said apology as it is only cosmetic and not
heartfelt, for the reason that conduct speaks for itself, and by
the conduct of the said respondent, when no action at all has been
taken against the person who may be responsible for non-processing
of the notice of this Court in such a serious matter, the apology
deserves to be rejected and is is so done. Accordingly, notice in
contempt  is  issued  to  Mr.  Vaibhav  Goyal,  the  Managing
Director/Chief Executive Officer of Navi General Insurance Limited.
The respondent shall show cause as to why appropriate action for
contempt of the order of this Court be not taken against him. The
respondent  shall  file  his  personal  affidavit  showing  cause.
However, personal appearance of the respondent is dispensed with,
for the present.
7. We find that the following respondents have not appeared
before the Court even today: respondent No. 45 – Kotak Mahindra
Life Insurance Company Limited; respondent No. 64 – Credit Access
Life Insurance Limited; respondent No. 77 – Zurich Kotak General
Insurance Company (India) Limited; respondent No. 89 – The New
India Assurance Company Limited; respondent No. 93 – Zuno General
Insurance Ltd.; respondent No. 95 – Aditya Birla Health Insurance
Co. Ltd.; and respondent No. 102 – General Insurance Corporation of

--- Page 60 ---
11
SLP (C) No. 5582/2023
India. Accordingly, notice in contempt is also issued against them.
On the next date, they shall file their affidavits showing cause as
to why the Court may not proceed against them and pass appropriate
orders for committing contempt of this Court. However, personal
appearance of the respondents is dispensed with, for the present,
except respondent No. 93.
8. Compliance affidavit has been filed by Mr. Parag Ved, whole-
time Director and Chief Executive Officer of respondent No. 79,
Liberty General Insurance Limited. His stand is that on 17th August
2026, he had booked a flight from Mumbai to Delhi. A copy of the
ticket is annexured to the said affidavit, which indicates that the
flight was to depart from Mumbai at 8:00 a.m. and reach Delhi at
10:20 a.m. However, it has been submitted that due to circumstances
beyond his control, he had missed the flight and thus could not be
physically present.
9. Having considered the same, we find that the reason for non-
appearance is bona  fide. Accordingly, accepting the unconditional
apology tendered by him, the issue relating to the present contempt
is closed against him. 
10. With regard to respondent No. 89, the New India Assurance
Company Limited, there is no explanation as to why the CMD/Chief
Executive Officer of the said company is not present. Accordingly,
notice in contempt is issued to the said respondent. The respondent
shall show cause as to why appropriate action for contempt of the
order of this Court be not taken. The respondent shall file an
affidavit showing cause. Personal appearance of the respondent is
dispensed with.

--- Page 61 ---
12
SLP (C) No. 5582/2023
11. With regard to respondent No. 64, Credit Access Life Insurance
Limited, the CMD/Chief Executive Officer is not present. It is
submitted by learned counsel that the post of CMD is vacant. We
find that there is no explanation as to why appearance was not
entered on behalf of respondent No. 64. The person heading the
concerned insurance company is directed to initiate appropriate
proceedings against the persons responsible for the same and bring
on record by way of an affidavit personally affirmed by the person
who is currently in charge of the affairs of the said insurance
company showing the fixing of responsibility and action taken
against the person responsible for non-compliance with the order of
the Court for which the Court had to pass a strict order for
appearance of the CMD.
12. With  regard  to  respondent  No.  77,  Zurich  Kotak  General
Insurance Company (India) Limited, Mr. Alok Kumar Agarwal, the
Managing Director & Chief Executive Officer, is present in Court.
Learned counsel submits that on 26th May 2026, inadvertently, the
name of the respondent has been arrayed as a party which had not
complied with the direction given by the Court on 6th April 2026,
though learned had marked his appearance.
13. Having regard to the aforesaid, the present issue against
respondent No. 77, Zurich Kotak General Insurance Company (India)
Limited stands closed.
14. Regarding respondent No. 79, on a query as to why, despite the
order dated 6th April 2026, directing for entering appearance, the
same was not done by 26th May 2026, the response is that they are
not even aware as to when actual notice was served. We find such

--- Page 62 ---
13
SLP (C) No. 5582/2023
explanation to be absolutely not worth even consideration for the
reason that if the CEO is unaware of what is happening in his
company, that too in a matter where there is an order of this
Court, we find there has been total casualness and lack of
responsibility shown on behalf of Mr. Parag Ved, Whole time
Director  and  Chief  Executing  Officer.  Accordingly,  notice  in
contempt is issued to the said respondent. The respondent shall
show cause as to why appropriate action for contempt of this Court
be not taken. The respondent shall file an affidavit showing cause.
However, personal appearance of the respondent is dispensed with,
for the present.
15. With regard to respondent No. 93, Zuno General Insurance

16. The Court takes strong exception to the statements made in
paragraphs No. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14. We are also
surprised as to how such defence is taken and justification sought
for her non-appearance which basically, as per the affidavit, is on
the ground that the Officer had a pre-scheduled official engagement
and it was extremely difficult to defer, reschedule or otherwise
rearrange the same, despite the fact that she has admitted that
notice of her appearance on 17.08.2026 had been received and she
was aware of it on 12.08.2026 itself, i.e., five days prior to the
said date.

the next date of hearing.

1. Heard Mr. Divyansh Tiwari, learned counsel for the
petitioner  and  Ms.  Astha  Sharma,  learned  counsel
appearing for the respondent/applicant.
2. Delay condoned.
3. In IA No.291609 of 2026 – a joint application has
been  filed for  directions under  Article 142  of the
Constitution of India in a disposed of Transfer Petition.
The Transfer Petition was disposed of on 30th August 2022.
By the said order, this Court transferred the proceedings
pending between the parties from Jalandhar, Punjab and
Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh to the Patiala House Courts,
Delhi.
1

--- Page 85 ---
4. The peculiar fact which has led to the filing of
the joint application for divorce in this Court is that
when the parties approached the Patiala House Courts with
an application under Section 13-B of the Hindu Marriage
Act, 1955, objections on jurisdiction were raised.
5. The marriage between the parties was solemnized on
7th June, 2017 and they have been living separately for
the last 7 years.
6. In view of the peculiar facts of the case and this
Court having already exercised jurisdiction to transfer
the cases and the parties being now handicapped from now
filing  a  petition  under  Section  13-B  of  the  Hindu
Marriage Act, 1955 in Delhi, we are inclined to entertain
the joint application filed for dissolution of marriage
here.
7. The  parties  have  entered  into  a  Settlement
Agreement dated 1 st June, 2026. The terms an d conditions

Courts for placing the same on record of the respective
cases and consign the files to the records.

Shipra Rai (wife) and Major Rajnikant Rai (husband). Ms.

CRIMINAL APPEAL No.______OF 2026

RENUKA JAIN                                     Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF NCT OF DELHI & ORS.                Respondent(s)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Ms. Fauzia Shakil, learned counsel for the
appellant; Mr. Davinder Pal Singh, learned A.S.G. assisted
by Mr. Akshat Aggarwal; and Ms. Vidhi Gupta, learned counsel
for the State of NCT of Delhi.  Mr. Vikas Sharma, learned
counsel has appeared for respondent no. 2.
3. Though respondent nos. 3 and 4 have been served, none has
appeared on their behalf.  Respondent no. 5 has not been
served. However, considering the nature of the order that we
propose to pass, service of notice upon respondent no. 5 may
not be necessary.
4. Appellant before us is the de facto complainant.  She had
lodged FIR No. 211/2017 before the Farsh Bazar Police Station
against the accused persons named therein under Section 420 of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (I.P.C.).
 
5. On completion of investigation, charge sheet has been
filed whereafter, the case has been registered as C.R. No.

--- Page 97 ---
7850/2019 and assigned to the Court of Judicial Magistrate
First Class in the Shahdara District Courts, Karkardooma,
Delhi (‘Trial Court’ hereinafter).
6. Aggrieved  by the  delay in  the trial,  appellant had
earlier moved the Delhi High Court (‘High Court’ for short) in
W.P. Criminal No. 2090/2018 wherein an order was passed by the
High Court on 07.02.2023 directing the Trial Court to conclude
the trial within two years after framing of charges.
7.  Since the trial did not progress much, a fresh petition
was filed by the appellant  before the High Court under Section
528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (B.N.S.S.)
corresponding  to  Section  482  of  the  Code  of  Criminal
Procedure, 1973 (Cr.P.C.) seeking a direction to the Trial
Court for expeditious disposal of the trial.
8. This time an objection was raised on behalf of the
prosecution questioning the locus standi of the appellant to
institute the proceedings.
9. Learned  Single  Judge  vide  the  impugned  order  dated
06.01.2026 concurred with the submissions made on behalf of
the prosecution that the role of the complainant is limited to
being a witness. Therefore, it is only the State or the
accused who can bring in such a petition. Paragraph 4 of the
impugned order reads thus:
“4. I find substance in the submission of the learned
prosecutor that the subject case being a State case,
role of the complainant de facto is limited to being a
witness and therefore, it is only the State or the
accused who can bring such petition. In this regard, it
would be apposite to also note that the complainant de
facto can sustain action independent of prosecution
side only in certain situations explicitly laid down in
law. The present petition does not fall under that
category.”
2.

--- Page 98 ---
9.1. After holding the petition to be a frivolous one and a
drain on the already overflowing dockets of the Court, the same
was dismissed by the High Court with cost of Rs.10,000/-
(Rupees Ten Thousand).
10. This Court by order dated 24.07.2026 had issued notice
while calling upon the learned standing counsel for the State
of NCT of Delhi to inform the Court on the next date i.e.
today as to the stage of the trial. In the meanwhile,
paragraph 6 of the impugned order imposing cost upon the
appellant was stayed.
11. In the hearing today, learned standing counsel submits
that prosecution has cited a total of 22 witnesses to be
examined, out of which one has been deleted.  Thus, there are
21  prosecution  witnesses.  PW-1  is  presently  being  cross
examined.
12. Detailed submissions have been made by learned counsel
for the parties which have been duly considered.
13. Section 301 Cr.P.C. provides for appearance of the Public
Prosecutor and pleading by him before any Court in respect of
a case of which he is in charge. He can do so without any
written authority. Sub-section (2) of Section 301 is relevant
and is extracted hereinunder:
“(2) If in any such case any private person instructs a
pleader to prosecute any person in any Court, the
Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor in
charge of the case shall conduct the prosecution, and
the pleader so instructed shall act therein under the
directions of the Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public
Prosecutor, and may, with the permission of the Court,
submit written arguments after the evidence is closed
in the case.”
3.

--- Page 99 ---
14. We may also refer to sub-section (2) of Section 302
Cr.P.C.  Section  302  deals  with  permission  to  conduct
prosecution.  Ordinarily, the prosecution is to be conducted
by  the  Public  Prosecutor  or  Assistant  Public  Prosecutor
without any written authority but any Magistrate  inquiring
into or trying a case may permit the prosecution to be
conducted by any person other than the police officer below the
rank of Inspector but no person other than the Advocate
General or Government Advocate or a Public Prosecutor or
Assistant Public Prosecutor shall be entitled to do so without
such permission. 
14.1. Sub-section(2) says that any person conducting the
prosecution may do so personally or by a pleader.
15. Section 24 Cr.P.C. deals with Public Prosecutors. As per
sub-section  (8),  the  Central  Government  or  the  State
Government, as the case may be, may appoint a Special Public
Prosecutor for the purposes of any case or class of cases.
Proviso to sub-section (8) of Section 24 Cr.P.C. empowers the
Trial Court to permit the victim to engage an advocate of his
choice to assist the prosecution.
16. Victim has been defined in Section 2(wa) Cr.P.C. to mean a
person who has suffered any loss or injury caused by reason of
the act or omission for which the accused person has been
charged and the expression  ‘victim’ inc ludes his or her
guardian or legal heir.
17. The aforesaid provisions find place in the B.N.S.S. as
well. Section 2(y) of the B.N.S.S. defines victim to mean a
person who has suffered any loss or injury caused by reason of
the act or omission of the accused person and includes the
4.

--- Page 100 ---
guardian or legal heir of such victim.
18. Likewise, Section 301 Cr.P.C. finds its manifestation in
Section 338 B.N.S.S.; so also sub-section (2) of Section 339
of B.N.S.S. contains the same provision as Section 302(2)
Cr.P.C.
19. From an analysis of the aforesaid provisions, it is
evident that a victim, as defined earlier in the Cr.P.C. and
now  in  the  B.N.S.S.,  is  not  a  stranger  to  a  criminal
proceeding in which he or she is th e sufferer  or the legal
guardian of such victim. The fact remains that it is due to
the loss or injury suffered by her at the hands of the accused
that has triggered the criminal process.
20. Therefore, to say that the role of the victim is limited
to being a witness, is not correct.  A victim or the legal
guardian of the victim is a definite stakeholder in the
criminal justice system. Like the accused, she has also a
vested right to insist on a speedy trial and also for a fair
trial. Therefore, on a reading of the statutory scheme as
enumerated supra, certainly a victim has locus standi to seek
a speedy trial. She can certainly bring a petition under
Section 528 B.N.S.S. seeking a direction from the High Court
to the Trial Court to expedite the trial proceedings.  
21. In Mangal Singh vs. Kishan Singh, (2009) 17 SCC 303,  this
Court, while recognising the right of a victim to insist on a
speedy trial, held that it would be a grave mistake to assume
that delay in trial does not cause acute suffering and anguish to
the victim of the offence. In many cases, the victim may suffer
even more than the accused. There is, therefore, no reason to
give all the benefits on account of the delay in the trial to the
accused and to completely deny all justice to the victim of the
5.

--- Page 101 ---
offence.
22. This Court highlighted the importance of a speedy trial for
both the accused and the victim in Rattiram vs. State of Madhya
Pradesh, (2012) 4 SCC 516. This Court emphasized that the whole
purpose of speedy trial is intended to avoid oppression and to
prevent  delay.  It  is  a  sacrosanct obligation  of  all
concerned with the justice dispensation system to see that
the administration of criminal justice becomes effective,
vibrant and meaningful.  Para 59 of the said decision is
extracted hereunder: 
"59. At this juncture, we would like to refer to two other
concepts, namely, speedy trial and treatment of a victim in
criminal jurisprudence based on the constitutional paradigm
and principle. The entitlement of the accused to speedy
trial has been repeatedly emphasised by this Court. It has
been recognised as an inherent and implicit aspect in the
spectrum of Article 21 of the Constitution. The whole
purpose of speedy trial is intended to avoid oppression and
prevent  delay.  It  is  a  sacrosanct  obligation  of  all
concerned with the justice dispensation system to see that
the administration of criminal justice becomes effective,
vibrant and meaningful. The concept of speedy trial cannot
be allowed to remain a mere formality (see Hussainara
Khatoon (1) v. State of Bihar [(1980) 1 SCC 81 and Raj Deo
Sharma v. State of Bihar (1998) 7 SCC 507].”
22.1. Insofar the right of the victim in a criminal trial
is concerned, this Court held that the right of a victim to
have a speedy trial cannot be overlooked. This Court held
thus:
“60. While delineating on the facets of speedy trial, it
cannot be regarded as an exclusive right of the accused.
The right of a victim has been given recognition in Mangal
Singh v. Kishan Singh [2009) 17 SCC 303] wherein it has
been observed thus: (SCC p. 307, para 14) "14.... Any
inordinate  delay  in  conclusion  of  a  criminal  trial
undoubtedly has a highly deleterious effect on the society
generally, and particularly on the two sides of the case.
But it will be a grave mistake to assume that delay in
trial does not cause acute suffering and anguish to the
victim of the offence. In many cases the victim may suffer
even more than the accused. There is, therefore, no reason
to give all the benefits on account of the delay in trial
6.

--- Page 102 ---
to the accused and to completely deny all justice to the
victim of the offence."
23. We may also gainfully refer to the observations made by
this Court in  Amir Hamza Shaikh vs. State of Maharashtra,
(2019) 8 SCC 387. Referring to the recommendations of the
Malimath Committee as well as to the amendment bought in to
the Cr.P.C. to provide a platform to the victim to assist the
Trial Court and to the three-Judge Bench decision of this
Court in J.K. International vs. State (NCT of Delhi), (2001) 3
SCC 462, where it has been held that the scheme in the Cr.P.C.
indicates that the person who is aggrieved by the offence
committed is not altogether wiped out from the scene of the
trial merely because the investigation was taken over by the
police, this Court held as under:
“9. This Court while considering the provisions of sub-
section (2) of Section 301 and Section 302 CrPC, held as
under: (J.K. International case, SCC pp. 465-67, paras 9-
12)
"9. The scheme envisaged in the Code of Criminal
Procedure indicates that a person who is aggrieved by
the offence committed, is not altogether wiped out from
the  scenario  of  the  trial  merely  because  the
investigation was taken over by the police and the
charge-sheet was laid by them. Even the fact that the
court  had  taken  cognizance  of  the  offence  is  not
sufficient to debar him from reaching the court for
ventilating his grievance. Even in the Sessions Court,
where the Public Prosecutor is the only authority
empowered to conduct the prosecution as per Section
225 of the Code, a private person who is aggrieved by
the offence involved in the case is not altogether
debarred from participating in the trial. This can be
discerned from Section 301(2) of the Code which reads
thus:
'301. (2) If in any such case any private person
instructs a pleader to prosecute any person in any
court,  the  Public  Prosecutor  or  Assistant  Public
Prosecutor in charge of the case shall conduct the
prosecution, and the pleader so instructed shall act
therein under the directions of the Public Prosecutor
or Assistant Public Prosecutor, and may, with the
permission  of  the  court,  submit  written  arguments
after the evidence is closed in the case.'
7.

--- Page 103 ---
     xxxxxxx
13. In J.K. International, it has been held that if the
cause of justice would be better served by granting such
permission, the Magistrate's Court would generally grant
such  permission.  An  aggrieved  private  person  is  not
altogether eclipsed from the scenario when the criminal
court take cognizance of the offences based on the report
submitted by the police.
       xxxxxxxx
15. In view of such principles laid down, we find that
though the Magistrate is not bound to grant permission at
the mere asking but the victim has a right to assist the
court in a trial before the Magistrate. The Magistrate may
consider as to whether the victim is in a position to
assist the court and as to whether the trial does not
involve such complexities which cannot be handled by the
victim. On satisfaction of such facts, the Magistrate would
be within his jurisdiction to grant permission to the
victim to take over the inquiry of the pendency before the
Magistrate.”
24. In the recent case of Keshvendra Singh vs. Shankar Singh,
2026 SCC Online SC 1588, this Court highlighted that the right
to speedy trial is not only the prerogative of the accused but
is also a valuable right of the victim. This Court analysed
the same in the following manner:
“23. "There is one more significant aspect of the matter.
Article 21 of the Constitution of India guarantees right to
speedy trial. This Court has held that right to speedy
trial is not only the prerogative of the accused but is
also a valuable right of the victim and any inordinate
delay  in  the  conclusion  of  the  trial,  could  have  a
deleterious  effect  on  the  society  in  general.  If  the
interpretation  canvassed  by  the  respondent-accused  is
accepted, it will render Section 12 of the Gangsters Act
ultra vires Article 21 of the Constitution of India. It
will also give a handle to the accused to delay all other
cases under the pretext that the proceedings are pending
under the Gangsters Act. Tremendous injustice will result
as with every day's delay, preservation of evidence will
become a challenge. Witnesses will be that much less
forthcoming and even if they are, with passage of time,
human memory would have begun to fade. This Court cannot
countenance any such interpretation which will make a
mockery of the judicial process.”
8.

--- Page 104 ---
25. That being the position, we are unable to agree with the
view taken by the High Court  castigating the victim for
bringing a petition before the Court seeking a speedy trial as
being completely frivolous and a drain on the overflowing
dockets of the Court. It is based on a complete misreading of
the  legal  and  constitutional  provisions  and  cannot  be
sustained.
26. We, therefore, set aside the impugned order of the High
Court dated 06.01.2026 and direct the Trial Court to conclude
the trial in C.R. Case No. 7850/2019 expeditiously and within
an outer limit of one year from today.  We clarify that we
have not expressed any opinion on the merits of the case and
all contentions are kept open.
27. The Criminal Appeal is, accordingly, allowed.
28.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

                             O R D E R
Heard learned Senior Counsel/Counsel for the parties.
2. Mr. S.V. Raju, learned Additional Solicitor General appearing
for the State of Maharashtra submits that he may be granted a
further period of three weeks to prepare a draft SOP with regard to
the production of undertrial prisoners before the Courts.
3. At this juncture, upon interaction with the learned counsel
for the parties, it appears to the Court that there is some
communication gap with regard to what the Court had in mind. The
intention of the Court is also to reduce the judicial workload of
the concerned Judicial Officers who, as a matter of formality, have
to take up the matter relating to the production of undertrial
prisoners and inquire whether the said undertrial prisoner has
anything to say with regard to his/her custody directly to the
Court, mainly in relation to any grievance which he/she may have.
4. Thus, it appears to the Court that if one Judicial Officer is
deputed to the local prison from where the undertrial prisoners are
to be produced before the Court, such Judicial Officer can complete
the formality of appearance before the Court of all such undertrial
prisoners in whose cases the said appearance is not for any other
reason but for the sole purpose of airing their grievance, if any,

--- Page 115 ---
9
and to inquire whether they are being treated as required in law.
5. This would serve two purposes. First, the concerned Judicial
Officer before whom the cases are pending would save time by not
having to undertake the mere formality of recording the presence of
the accused concerned and asking whether he/she has any grievance
to make before the Court. Thus, if, on an average, 20-30 undertrial
prisoners are to be brought to the Court only for the purpose of
inquiring into their condition, the deputation of one Judicial
Officer to the concerned local prison to record the same would save
the judicial time of the Court seized of their cases, while such
judicial work would be performed by the deputed Judicial Officer.
5.1. Secondly, there would be no question of any additional burden
on the judicial side by deputing one Judicial Officer for the said
purpose, as that Judicial Officer would be performing the judicial
work of the Judicial Officer concerned, who would thereby be able
to proceed with the other cases listed before him/her.
6. It can also be worked out that depending on the number of
cases, such deputation of a Judicial Officer from the Civil Court
to the prison may be limited to a few hours, half a day or the
whole  day.  All  the  Stakeholders,  especially  the  States/Union
Territories and the High Courts may take a call on the same. The
Court  is  conscious  that  in  some  cases  where  the  number  of
undertrial  prisoners  is  small,  the  arrangement  of  physical
production may be more feasible and practical and may be continued.
The said exercise be undertaken within four weeks.
7. For the said exercise, all the States/Union Territories and
the High Courts shall submit their suggestions to the Nodal

--- Page 116 ---
10
Officer. We request Mr. S.V. Raju, learned Additional Solicitor
General, to also go through the same and come up with common areas
on which the Court may issue certain immediate directions, as also
other areas where there may be a need for further deliberation.
The matter be deliberated upon between the Government of the
State/Union Territory concerned and the High Court concerned and
thereafter, a joint report, by way of an affidavit, be submitted
after service of a copy thereof upon the Nodal Officer, latest
within four weeks from today.
8. The Nodal Officer and Mr. S.V. Raju, learned Additional
Solicitor General are requested to go through the same and submit a
consolidated report within four weeks thereafter.
9. The matters be listed on 01.12.2026 at 02:00 p.m.
  (SAPNA BISHT)                                 (ANJALI PANWAR)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. By our order dated 21.07.2026, we had granted six
weeks’ time to the State of Bihar to ensure that each and
every unauthorized structure/construction and encroachments
standing on the flood plains are removed between Nauzar Ghat
to Nurpur in Patna. 
2. We also restrained the authorities from proceeding
further  with  some  construction  which  is  blocking  the
ecological flow of water. This construction, which the State
intends to undertake may lead to shrinking of the river
Yamuna channel in Vrindavan District, Mathura, State of
Uttar Pradesh. The construction shall not proceed further at
any cost.
3. Today,  when  the  matter  was  taken  up  for  further
hearing, Mr. S.D. Sanjay, the learned Advocate General
appearing for the State of Bihar would submit that the
directions issued by this Court have been partially complied
with. There are many unauthorized structures/constructions
yet to be removed from the flood plains. According to him,
the recent natural calamity in Nepal which led to the level
of river Ganga rising has submerged this entire portion and
this made it difficult for the authorities to proceed
further with the removal of the encroachments.
4. We grant for one last time, eight weeks’ time period to
comply with our directions, failing which, we shall have to
4

--- Page 121 ---
summon the Chief Secretary of the State of Bihar and other
authorities before us and we may also proceed further with
contempt. 
5. There are few intervention applications before us.
These intervenors have to say that whatever construction is
there, is on their own land and those do not fall within the
flood plains. In this regard, it may be open for these
intervenors  to  prefer  an  appropriate  representation
addressed to the competent authority. 
6. If any representation is preferred by any one of the
intervenors before us, along with their representation, the
intervenor shall attach all documents of his title over the
land, including the authorized sanction/ permission and
authorization of building that might have been granted to
him for the purpose of construction of any building. In the
absence of these documents, no representation shall be
looked into. 
7. The intervention applications stand disposed of.
8. After eight weeks, i.e., on the next date of hearing,
we want a full compliance report as regards the removal of
the encroachments as directed by us. No further time shall
be granted.
9. List on 08th October, 2026 at 03:00 P.M..

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
     CIVIL APPEAL NOS.          OF 2026
     (Arising out of SLP(C) Nos. 12010-12011 of 2025)
BALASHANMUGAM                                  APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
MAYANGATHAL & ORS.                                RESPONDENTS
R1 : MAYANGATHAL 
R2 : PONNAMMAL
R3 : RUCKMANI
O R D E R
Heard Mr. Raghenth Basant, learned senior counsel for the
appellant  and  Ms.  Nina  R.  Nariman,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondents.
2. Leave granted.
3. These  present  appeals  arise  out  of  the  common  impugned
judgment dated 03.01.2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Madras in S.A. Nos.840 and 847 of 2021 and C.M.P. No.16173 of 2021,
by which, the judgment and decree dated 28.07.2021 in A.S. No.81 of
2020 and A.S. No.83 of 2020 passed by the learned Principal
District Court, Tiruppur upholding the decree and judgment dated
20.03.2020 in O.S. No.367 of 2016 and Interim Application No.35 of
2018 in E.P. No.14 of 2017 in O.S. No.213 of 2002 passed by the
Sub-Court, Aviashi, was set aside.

--- Page 137 ---
2
4. Learned senior counsel for the appellant submits that in a
joint property, the appellant had bought the undivided half share
on  31.01.1989  under  a  Court  auction.  Thereafter,  as  actual
partition had not happened, matters lingered. It was the contention
of the learned senior counsel that on 29.04.2002, the appellant
filed a suit for partition in which, the mother of the respondents,
who was the original defendant had appeared. However, subsequently,
she did not participate and the matter was proceeded ex-parte. On
25.07.2003, a preliminary decree was also drawn up. The mother of
the  respondents  passed  away  on  30.09.2007.  Thereafter,  the
respondents were impleaded by the appellant in the said suit
sometime in the year 2008. It was contended that in the said suit,
upon appearing, the respondents agreed to the 50% demarcation of
their share. However, the difference was with regard to the actual
demarcation. The respondents, agreed to accept the division, on the
condition that the entire eastern portion of the property be
allotted to them and the western portion to the appellant. The same
was objected and a Court Commissioner was deputed. The Court
Commissioner gave a report and with a proposal to demarcate the
land, copy of which is at page no.71 of the brief. In the same,
according to the learned senior counsel for the appellant, there
was equitable partition inasmuch as, major portion of the east,
which had a main road abutting was given in favour of the
respondents whereas, about 1/3rd portion of the same was to be given
to the appellant. However, the same was not acceptable and the
respondents filed another substantive suit in the year 2010.
Thereafter, the Trial Court in the suit filed by the appellant

--- Page 138 ---
3
passed a final decree and judgment in terms of the report of the
Court Commissioner. The same was never challenged. After passing of
the final decree, the respondents in the suit filed in the year
2010 sought an amendment in the year 2017 in which, both the
preliminary and the final decree were challenged.
5. The suit filed by the respondents was dismissed by an order
dated 20.03.2020 and the Objection filed by the respondents in the
Execution Case filed by the appellant was also dismissed on the
same day. This led to the respondents filing two appeals against
the said two orders, which were dismissed by two separate orders on
28.07.2021 by the learned Principal District Court, Tiruppur.
Thereafter, the respondents preferred Second Appeals No. 840 and
847 of 2021, which have been allowed by the High Court vide the
common impugned judgment.
6. This according to learned senior counsel for the appellant was
misconceived and in fact, not justified, both on facts as well as
in law. It was submitted that the major ground on which the Second
Appeals of the respondents have been allowed by the High Court is
that the appellant had committed a fraud by not impleading the
respondents in his suit. To this, the reply of the learned senior
counsel  for  the  appellant  is  that  when  the  mother  of  the
respondents was already a defendant in the suit filed by the
appellant in the year 2002 and subsequent thereto, upon her death
in the year 2007, in the year 2008 the respondents were impleaded,
there is no question of any fraud being committed as there was no
omission in the eyes of law as the interest of the respondents was
already being espoused by their late mother. It was further

--- Page 139 ---
4
contended that the High Court has also erred in directing the
appellant to file a fresh suit which would mean that the clock is
turned back and a purchase made by the appellant, which is
undisputed, in January, 1989, the fruits of the same will not be
available to the appellant in the near foreseeable future.
7. Learned counsel for the respondents submitted that the Court
has always taken a strict view whenever fraud is involved. It was
submitted that though the respondents may have appeared before the
Court in the suit filed by the appellant, but it did not preclude
them from raising issues which had happened in the past and the
appellant could not run away from his conduct. It was submitted
that initially, the respondents had agreed to the partition only
for the sake of settling the issue once and for all and only to
ensure equitable distribution inasmuch as, the eastern portion had
been fully developed and nurtured by them by not only making
construction but also planting coconut trees, which are now fully
grown up and which also has two bore wells and a well. It was
further contended that the appellant was silent/unconcerned about
his rights from the year 1989 and had suddenly woken up in the year
2002 and thus, had acquiesced to his position and now, cannot seek
eviction of the respondents from the portion they have been in
possession  of  since  the  beginning.  Learned  counsel  further
submitted that despite being a necessary party right from the time
when the suit was filed in the year 2002 by the appellant, since a
partition had already been taken place between the mother and the
daughters,  they  were  necessary  parties  as  also  a  registered
settlement was in existence at that point of time. Thus, according

--- Page 140 ---
5
to learned counsel, on this point alone, the impugned judgment
needs no interference.
8. In  response,  learned  senior  counsel  for  the  appellant
submitted that factually, the submissions of the learned counsel
for the respondents may not be correct as the respondents had not
raised any objection with regard to the conduct of the appellant,
when they appeared upon impleadment in the suit filed by the
appellant. It was also contended that the well is totally in the
portion allotted to the respondents along with one bore well. It
was  contended  that  at  best,  the  respondents  can  claim  some
compensation for the bore well which was constructed by them and as
per the Trial Court and the Appellate Court, allotted in the share
of the appellant, but they cannot retain the portion on which the
said bore well stands constructed.
9. In response to the third objection of the learned counsel for
the respondents with regard to the respondents not being made party
despite being necessary party, learned senior counsel for the
appellant submits that the said partition itself was ab initio void
for the reason that the partition on the ground could only be of a
property which is demarcated by metes and bounds and at that point
of time, the appellant had an undivided 50% of the share and
without his share being demarcated first, any subsequent partition
is meaningless in the eyes of law.
10. Having considered the matter in its entirety, the Court finds
that the matter needs to be given a quietus once and for all. In
this regard, the Court finds that the basic bone of contention
today between the parties is to the actual demarcation on the

--- Page 141 ---
6
ground as to how their share of 3.34 acres each, which is not
disputed, is actually apportioned between the two sides. 
11. We have given our anxious thoughts to the entire controversy
and have also gone through the sketch/image/diagram on record, both
regarding the claim of the respondents and the portion allotted to
the parties by the Trial Court and upheld by the Appellate Court.
In our considered opinion, we find that the apportionment made by
the Trial Court and upheld by the Appellate Court, is fair and just
and ought not to have been interfered with.
12. Accordingly  on  the  said  short  point,  these  appeals  are
allowed. The common impugned judgment dated 03.01.2025 passed by
the High Court of Judicature at Madras in S.A. Nos.840 and 847 of
2021 and C.M.P. No.16173 of 2021 are set aside. The judgment and
decree passed by the Trial Court and upheld by the Appellate Court
stands restored and the execution shall take place in terms of the
report submitted by the Court Commissioner, which has been accepted
in the final decree of the Trial Court dated 30.10.2012 and upheld
by the Appellate Court.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
