IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
 CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP(CRIMINAL) NO.10376/2025]
    MUNNA MANDAVI                             APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
    STATE OF CHHATTISGARH                     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1.    Leave granted.
2. The appellant before this Court has filed the
present criminal appeal arising out of Special Leave
Petition  (Criminal)  No.10376/2025,  challenging  his
conviction in connection with FIR No.10/2017 dated
29.12.2017,  registered  at  Police  Station  Puspal,
District  Sukma,  for  the  offence  punishable  under
Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short,
“IPC”).
3. As  per  the  prosecution  case,  the  appellant
herein, Munna Mandavi, lost his son. He suspected one
Somaru, who was allegedly practising black magic, of
being responsible for his son's death. The appellant
went  to  the  house  of  Somaru and  assaulted  him.
Unfortunately, Somaru succumbed to his injuries. There
were a large number of prosecution witnesses in the

--- Page 169 ---
2
matter. The trial court convicted the appellant for the
offences punishable under Section 302 of the IPC and
Section 5 of the Chhattisgarh Tonhi Pratadna Niwaran
Adhiniyam,  2005.  The  trial  court  relied  upon  the
testimony of PW-5,  Sunny Mandavi , and PW-6,  Fagani
Mandavi, who attributed the act of assault with an axe
to the appellant. The trial court also rejected the
defence contention that PW-5 was not present at the
spot.
4. Learned  counsel  appearing  on  behalf  of  the
appellant vehemently argued before this Court that the
entire trial stands vitiated, as the evidence of PW-2
to PW-6 was recorded in the absence of the appellant,
in violation of the statutory provision contained in
Section 273 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
(for short, “Cr.P.C.”). He submitted that the appellant
was not on bail and that it was the duty of the State
to produce the accused/appellant, particularly on the
dates on which the evidence was being recorded. Learned
counsel for the appellant placed reliance upon the
judgments of this Court in  Naresh Kumar v. State of
Delhi, 2024 (7) SCALE 219 , and Atma Ram v. State of
Rajasthan, (2019) 20 SCC 481.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the State argued
before  this  Court  that,  in  Atma  Ram  (supra),  an
objection had been raised by the defence counsel when

--- Page 170 ---
3
the witnesses were being examined in the absence of the
accused,  whereas,  in  the  present  case,  no  such
objection was raised by the defence counsel.
6. We have carefully gone through the entire record
of the case. We are dealing with a case concerning a
poor tribal who is not aware with the legal provisions
and who, with great difficulty, engages a lawyer.
Another important  aspect of  the case  is that  the
District Jail is hardly 3 kilometres away from the
District Court. Nothing prevented the prosecution from
producing the appellant before the trial court during
the  trial,  particularly  when  the  evidence  of  the
witnesses was being recorded, and the statements were
recorded behind his back.
7. Section 273 of the Cr.P.C. reads as under:-
“273. Evidence to be taken in presence of
accused.-  Except  as  otherwise  expressly
provided, all evidence taken in the course of
the trial or other proceeding shall be taken in
the presence of the accused, or, when his
personal attendance is dispensed with, in the
presence of his pleader:
[Provided that where the evidence of a woman
below the age of eighteen years who is alleged
to have been subjected to rape or any other
sexual offence, is to be recorded, the court
may take appropriate measures to ensure that
such woman is not confronted by the accused
while at the same time ensuring the right of
cross-examination of the accused.]
Explanation.  -  In  this  Section,  "accused"
includes a person in relation to whom any

--- Page 171 ---
4
proceeding  under  Chapter  VIII  has  been
commenced under this Code.”
8. The aforesaid statutory provision of law makes it
abundantly clear that all evidence taken in the course
of the trial or other proceedings shall be taken in the
presence  of  the  accused  or,  when  his  personal
attendance has been dispensed with, in the presence of
his pleader. In the present case, the accused was in
custody, and therefore, the question of dispensing with
his  personal  attendance  does  not  arise.  Meaning
thereby, all evidence was required to be taken in the
course of the trial in the presence of the accused. The
same, however, has not been done. Therefore, the entire
trial stands vitiated.
9. In  light  of  the  aforesaid,  the  judgment  of
conviction dated 01.11.2021 passed in Sessions Trial
No.119/2018  by  the  learned  Sessions  Judge,  South
Bastar,  Dantewada  and  the  judgment  affirming  the
conviction passed by the High Court dated 03.01.2025 in
CRA No.1520 of 2021 are hereby set aside.  The matter
is remanded back to the trial court to conduct a de
novo trial.  The trial court shall conclude the trial
after following the procedure prescribed under the Code
of Criminal Procedure.
10. Learned counsel for the appellant has placed
reliance upon a judgment reported in Naresh Kumar Vs.

--- Page 172 ---
5
State of Delhi 2024 (7) SCALE 219 to contend that in
the light of the aforesaid judgment and keeping in view
the period of incarceration, the appellant should be
released forthwith and no  de novo  trial should be
ordered.  This Court after going through the aforesaid
judgment is of the view that in the case of  Naresh
Kumar (supra), the appellant Naresh Kumar therein has
suffered incarceration for more than 12 years and the
incident occurred more than 29 years ago. The present
case is distinguishable on facts.  In the present case,
the incident is dated 29.12.2017 and the trial court
has convicted the appellant on 01.11.2021.  The appeal
was dismissed by the High Court on 03.01.2025 and
therefore, keeping in view the aforesaid, the Naresh
Kumar judgment does not help the appellant at all as it
was passed in the peculiar facts and circumstances of
that case.
11. Resultantly, the appeal is allowed. The trial
Court is directed to conduct a  de novo  trial by
examining all the witnesses afresh in the presence of
the  appellant/accused.   The  appellant  has  already
served a sentence of 9 years and, therefore, he is
directed to be released on bail forthwith subject to
terms and conditions as may be imposed by the trial
court.

--- Page 173 ---
6
12. Pending application (s), if any, shall stand
disposed of. 
…………………………………………………………………J.

2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal arises out of an order dated

Principal Seat at Jabalpur in Criminal Appeal No.3030 of
2014, by which, the High Court has dismissed the appeal
of the appellant herein and upheld the judgment dated

Jabalpur in S.S.T.No. 88/2013, convicting the appellant
for the offence punishable under Sections 366 and 376(2)
(i) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short the ‘IPC’)

DHRUVO KUMAR DAS APPELLANT
                        VERSUS
STATE OF UTTARAKHAND     RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant, who has been arraigned as an accused for
the offences punishable under Sections 302 and 201 of
the  Indian  Penal  Code,  1860,  came  to  be  tried  by  the
learned  Third  Additional  District  &  Sessions  Judge  in
Sessions T rial No.30/2020 and accepting the case of the
1

--- Page 185 ---
prosecution wherein it was alleged that appellant had an
illicit relationship with the deceased Priya Bala and based
on  circumstantial  evidence,  appellant  came  to  be
convicted by judgment dated 02.12.2023 and sentenced
him to life imprisonment with a fine of Rs.50,000/- under
Section  302  of  the  IPC  and  four  years’  rigorous
imprisonment with a fine of Rs.10,000/- under Section 201
of the IPC and ordered the sentences to run concurrently .
An appeal has been filed in Criminal Appeal No.889/2023
challenging  the  judgment  of  conviction  alongwith  an
application for suspension of sentence and grant of bail.
By the impugned order, the jurisdictional High Court has
rejected the said application based on the appreciation of
the  evidence  that  had  been  laid  before  the  trial  court.
Hence, this appeal. 
4. We have heard the learned counsels appearing for
the parties and perused the counter-affidavit filed by the
State whereunder it has been contended that appellant
before being apprehended was in the process of fleeing
out of the country and as such if any leniency is extended
2

--- Page 186 ---
to  him  there  is  likelihood  of  appellant  absconding  and
there is flight risk.
5. Per contra, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
appellant would  draw the attention  of the Court  to the
testimony  of  the  witnesses  who  had  been  examined
before  trial  court  to  highlight  the  infirmities  in  the
prosecution case and would also contend that prolonged
incarceration is yet another ground for grant of bail by
suspending the sentence. He would also submit that as
per FIR records, the alleged incident having occurred from
12.09.2019 to 23.09.2019 and the column in the FIR for
the cause for delay in lodging the FIR is left blank. On this
ground  also,  he  seeks  for  the  suspension  of  grant  of
sentence and grant of bail.
6. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the
parties and on perusal of the entire records placed before
this Court, we are of the considered view that appellant is
entitled for suspension of sentence and grant of bail for
the reason that hearing of the appeal is likely to take long
time  and  also  the  fact  that  appellant  has  suffered
3

--- Page 187 ---
incarceration of more than seven years. Though we are
tempted  to  look  into  the  purported  infirmities  in  the
prosecution case which is sought to be highlighted by the
learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant,  we
desist from doing so as it is likely to prejudice the case of
the prosecution in the pending appeal and as such without
commenting upon the so-called infirmities and leaving it
open to be adjudicated by the appellate court where the
criminal  appeal  is  pending,  this  appeal  is  allowed  by
setting  aside  the  impugned  order  and  directing  that
sentence  imposed  on  the  appellant  in  Sessions  T rial
No.30/2020 dated 28.02.2020 stands suspended and he is
ordered  to  be  released  on  bail  on  such  terms  and
conditions as the learned Sessions Judge may deem fit to
impose including the condition of directing the appellant
to produce two local solvent sureties of Rs.50,000/- each.
The trial court would be at liberty to impose such other
and  further  conditions  as  it  deems  fit  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of the present case.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
 CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF   SLP (CRIMINAL) NO.17493/2026  ]  
KALLU @ MADUSUDAN SHARMA & ORS.            APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
     THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH                RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1.   Leave granted.
2. The present appeal arises out of the impugned
judgment of conviction dated 05.08.2026 passed by the
High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior (for short,
“the High Court”) in Criminal Appeal No.1026 of 2016,
whereby the appellants have been convicted for the
offence punishable under Section 302 read with Section
34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and sentenced to
undergo rigorous imprisonment for life, with a fine of
Rs.10,000/- each, and, in default of payment of fine,
to undergo simple imprisonment for one year.
3. Learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellants, at the outset, has drawn the attention of
this Court to the order dated 20.07.2026 passed by the
High Court. The same reads as under:

--- Page 199 ---
2
“This Criminal Appeal under Section 374 (2) of
Cr.P.C. has been filed against the judgment and
sentence dt.23.09.2016 passed by the Second
Additional  Sessions  Judge,  Gohad,  District
Bhind M.P. in Sessions Trial No.303/2013.
On 16.07.2026, following order was passed :-
In view of the order passed in CRA
No.111/2017, list this case for final
hearing at motion stage on 20.07.2026
alongwith  CRA  No.111/2017.  The  case
shall  be  taken  up  at  2:30  PM
irrespective of the serial number at
which it might be listed.
Today Shri M.L. Yadav submitted that he has not
prepared the case and prays for adjournment.
When his attention was drawn towards the order
dt. 16.07.2026, then it was submitted by him
that since an order of final hearing was passed
in  connected  case,  therefore,  he  has  not
prepared the case.
He was requested to read the prosecution story
from paragraph 3 of the judgment but instead of
doing that, he has started looking at the Court
and did not utter a single word. Thus, it is
clear that counsel for the appellant is merely
interested in arguing the bail applications but
is not ready to even read out paragraph 3 of
the judgment containing the prosecution case.
Be that whatever it may be.
The only question for consideration is as to
whether this Court should adjourn the matter on
account of non-cooperation by counsel for the
appellants or not and whether counsel for the
appellants can be permitted to hijack the court
proceedings  specifically  when  by  order  dt.
16.07.2026, it was pointed out that the matter
shall be heard finally on 29.07.2026.

--- Page 200 ---
3
The Supreme Court in the case of Surya Baksh
Singh v. State of U.P., reported in (2014) 14
SCC 222 has held as under:
24. It seems to us that it is necessary
for  the  appellate  court  which  is
confronted  with  the  absence  of  the
convict as well as his counsel, to
immediately proceed against the persons
who stood surety at the time when the
convict was granted bail, as this may
lead to his discovery and production in
court. If even this exercise fails to
locate and bring forth the convict, the
appellate court is empowered to dismiss
the appeal. We fully and respectfully
concur with the recent elucidation of
the law, profound yet perspicuous, in
K.S. Panduranga v. State of Karnataka.
After  a  comprehensive  analysis  of
previous decisions our learned Brother
had distilled the legal position into
six propositions: (SCC p. 734, para 19)
"19.1.  that  the  High  Court  cannot
dismiss an appeal for non-prosecution
simpliciter  without  examining  the
merits; 
19.2. that the Court is not bound to
adjourn  the  matter  if  both  the
appellant  or  his  counsel/lawyer  are
absent;
19.3. that the court may, as a matter
of prudence or indulgence, adjourn the
matter but it is not bound to do so;
19.4, that it can dispose of the appeal
after perusing the record and judgment
of the trial court.
19.5. that if the accused is in jail
and cannot, on his own, come to court,
it would be advisable to adjourn the
case and fix another date to facilitate
the appearance of the appellant-accused
if his lawyer is not present, and if
the lawyer is absent and the court
deems  it  appropriate  to  appoint  a
lawyer at the State expense to assist

--- Page 201 ---
4
it, nothing in law would preclude the
court from doing so; and
19.6. that if the case is decided on
merits in the absence of the appellant,
the  higher  court  can  remedy  the
situation."
Therefore, one of the recognized mode of disposal
of appeal is to go through the record and decide
the matter. In the present case, appellants are
being represented by the counsel but the counsel
are not ready to argue.
Under these circumstances, this Court is left with
no other option but to go through the record.
Accordingly,  record  was  gone  through  and  the
counsel for the State was heard.
Reserved for judgment.”
4. He has vehemently argued before this Court that an
adjournment was sought in the matter by the learned counsel
appearing for the appellants on the ground that, in a
connected case, i.e., Sessions Trial No.303 of 2013, an
order had been passed for final hearing and, therefore, as
no such order had been passed in the present case, he was
not prepared to argue the matter. Accordingly, time was
sought to prepare and argue the case. However, the High
Court declined the request for adjournment and proceeded to
decide the matter on merits.
5. The High Court, while deciding the matter on merits,
relied upon the judgment delivered in Surya Baksh Singh v.
State of U.P. , reported in (2014) 14 SCC 222. We have
carefully gone through the aforesaid judgment. In our
opinion, if the learned counsel was not ready to argue the
matter, an Amicus Curiae ought to have been appointed to

--- Page 202 ---
5
assist the Court and argue the matter on behalf of the
appellants. In fact, nobody had argued the matter on behalf
of the appellants before the High Court, and the High
Court,  after  going  through  the  record,  dismissed  the
criminal appeal.
6. Learned senior counsel appearing for the appellants
has placed reliance upon the judgment delivered in Chandra
Pratap Singh v. The State of Madhya Pradesh, 2023 INSC 887,
and has contended that the matter may be remanded back to
the High Court for fresh consideration. 
7. This  Court,  after  careful  consideration  of  the
aforesaid judgments and the fact that nobody had argued the
appeal on behalf of the appellants, is of the view that the
matter deserves to be remanded back to the High Court for
fresh consideration. Accordingly, the matter is remanded
back to the High Court to decide the appeal afresh. In the
event that the counsel appearing for the appellants is not
available, the High Court shall be at liberty to appoint an
Amicus Curiae to assist the Court and thereafter decide the
matter on merits, in accordance with law. The appellants
have already surrendered and shall remain in custody till
the matter is decided afresh by the High Court. As  this
Court is not passing any order in respect of suspension of
sentence, the High Court is requested to decide the matter
as expeditiously as possible at an early date.

--- Page 203 ---
6
8. With  the  above  observations  and  directions,  the
appeal stands disposed of.    
9. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION NO. 35 OF 2025
FINECURE PHARMACEUTICAL LIMITED PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
SPIRIT PHARMACEUTICAL LLC & ANR. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This petition under Section 11(9) of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act, 1996 (1996 Act), seeks the appointment of a sole
arbitrator to adjudicate disputes arising from a Manufacturing and
Supply  Agreement  (MSA)  dated  11.03.2022  read  with  Exclusive
Relation Agreement (ERA) dated 11.03.2022 (collectively referred to
as  ‘Agreements’),  executed  between  the  Petitioner  and  the
Respondent No. 1.
2. Briefly stated, the Petitioner is a public limited company
having its registered office in India, engaged in the business of
manufacturing and marketing of pharmaceutical formulations and
nutraceuticals in the dosage form of tablets, syrups, powders,
injections etc. Respondent No. 1 is a limited liability company
incorporated under the laws of the United States of America,
engaged in the business of marketing, promotion, and distribution
of a wide range of pharmaceutical products. Respondent No. 2 is
also a company incorporated under the laws of the United States of
America, involved in the business of manufacturing, marketing and
distribution of drugs. 
1

--- Page 206 ---
3. The  Petitioner  and  Respondent  No.  1  entered  into  the
Agreements  for  the  manufacturing  of  specified  products  on  a
principal-to-principal basis; and the same were to be marketed,
sold, and distributed by Respondent No. 1 within the territory of
the United States of America. Under the Agreements, the parties
agreed that all disputes arising out of or in connection with the
Agreements shall be referred to arbitration in accordance with
Clause 16 of the MSA read with Clause 17 of the ERA. The said
clauses, which are governed by the laws of India, provide that a
dispute not resolved through amicable consultations within sixty
days may be referred to arbitration, which is to be conducted in
the English language in accordance with the 1996 Act, with New
Delhi as the place of arbitration.
4. It appears that a dispute arose in the year 2024 when
Respondent No. 1 allegedly defaulted on its payment obligations
towards  the  consignments  manufactured  and  supplied  by  the
Petitioner. According to the Petitioner, a sum of USD 1,583,567.53
(excluding  interest  and  other  consequential  reliefs)  remains
outstanding against invoices raised between March 2024 and October
2024. Under these circumstances, the Petitioner issued a notice of
default dated 03.10.2024 followed by a notice of termination dated
14.10.2024 calling upon Respondent No. 1 to clear the outstanding
dues. Upon the alleged failure of Respondent No. 1 to do so, the
Petitioner sought to initiate arbitral proceedings in terms of the
dispute resolution clause contained in the Agreements.
2

--- Page 207 ---
5. Consequently, the Petitioner issued a notice dated 18.10.2024
to  Respondent  No.  1,  invoking  the  arbitration  clause  for
appointment of a Sole Arbitrator. 
6. During this period, Respondent No. 2 purportedly acquired the
assets and business operations of Respondent No. 1 through a sale
process initiated by a secured lender of Respondent No. 1. The
Petitioner contends that since Respondent No. 2 has stepped into
the shoes of Respondent No. 1, it is liable for its dues, whereas
Respondent No. 2 is stated to contest this, claiming to have
acquired the assets free of liabilities. 
7. As Respondent No. 1 failed to respond to the said notice, the
Petitioner has filed the instant Petition under Section 11 of the
1996 Act. The Petitioner impleaded Respondent No. 2 stating it to
be a necessary party as it is jointly and severally liable for the
debt.
8. The Petitioner has also instituted petitions under Section 9
of the 1996 Act before the High Court of Delhi, being O.M.P.(I)
(Comm.) No. 366 of 2024 and O.M.P.(I)(Comm.) No. 420 of 2024. In
the former, by order dated 24.10.2024, Respondent No. 1 was
restrained,  till  the  next  date  of  hearing,  from  selling,
transferring  or  alienating  its  assets  to  the  extent  of  USD
1,583,567.53. Both petitions are stated to be pending.
3

--- Page 208 ---
9. We have heard learned Counsel for the parties, and perused the
material placed on record.
10. The existence of the arbitration agreements contained in
Clause 16 of the MSA and Clause 17 of the ERA is evident from the
record, and the notice invoking arbitration dated 18.10.2024 is
stated  to  have  remained  unanswered.  Since  the  Petitioner  is
incorporated in India while the Respondents are incorporated in the
United States of America, the arbitration is an international
commercial arbitration within the meaning of Section 2(1)(f) of the
1996 Act, for which this Court is the designated forum under
Section 11. The scope of our enquiry at this stage being confined
to the prima facie existence of an arbitration agreement, all other
issues are for determination by the Arbitral Tribunal.
11. Keeping in view the facts and circumstances recorded above and
the relevant provision(s) under the Agreements, we deem it just and
appropriate to allow the instant Arbitration Petition and appoint
Justice Siddharth Mridul, former Chief Justice of the High Court of
Manipur, as the Sole Arbitrator to resolve the subsisting disputes
between the parties arising out of and in connection with the
Agreements. The seat and venue of arbitration, in accordance with
the  arbitration  agreements,  shall  be  New  Delhi,  India.  The
arbitration  shall  be  conducted  in  the  English  language  in
accordance with the 1996 Act.
4

--- Page 209 ---
12. The Petitioner has alleged that Respondent No. 2, though not a
signatory  to  the  Agreements,  has  stepped  into  the  shoes  of
Respondent No. 1 and is jointly and severally liable for its dues,
and has also reserved the right to implead other entities. Whether
Respondent No. 2 or any other person is bound by the arbitration
agreements, and whether any other party can be joined to the
arbitral proceedings, shall be decided by the learned Arbitrator in
accordance with law, including the issues under Section 16 of the
1996 Act, uninfluenced by anything stated herein.
13. All the objections raised by the parties are left open to be
urged before the learned Arbitrator, including, without limitation,
objections  as  to  jurisdiction,  arbitrability,  limitation,
compliance with the pre-arbitral consultation requirement under
Clauses 16.2 and 16.3 of the MSA and Clauses 17.2 and 17.3 of the
ERA, and the effect of the sale of the assets of Respondent No. 1
on the claims raised. It is made clear that we have not made any
observations on the merits of the dispute(s). The petitions pending
before the High Court of Delhi under Section 9 of the 1996 Act
shall be decided by that Court independently, in accordance with
law, uninfluenced by this order.
14. The Arbitrator shall have the liberty to fix his/her own
remuneration/fees in consultation with the parties. The fees and
expenses of the arbitration shall be borne in accordance with the
arbitration agreements, subject to the final determination of costs
in the award.
5

--- Page 210 ---
15. The Registry is directed to communicate a copy of this order
to the learned Arbitrator, and to the parties, within one week.
Ordered accordingly.
16. Pending  interlocutory  applications,  if  any,  also  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 25567 OF 2025)
DEVENDRA NATH MISHRA & ORS. APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
RAVI BAJPAI     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  present  appeal  arises  out  of  the  order
07.03.2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad in Matters Under Article 227 No. 1363 of 2024.
3. The undisputed facts of the case reveal that the
appellant/landlord  acquired  ownership  of  the  subject
property on 10.07.1984. Following the purchase, a statutory
notice was issued under Section 21(1)(a) of the Act, 1972 1
requiring the tenant to vacate the premises upon the expiry
of three years.
1 .   Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (regulation of Letting, Rent
and Eviction) Act, 1972
1

--- Page 213 ---
4. Despite statutory notice and assurances given before
the Prescribed Authority as far back as in 1988, the
respondent-tenant failed to vacate the premises. As the
appellant required the premises bona fide to establish a
medical clinic for his neurosurgeon son, proceedings were
initiated, being Original Suit No. 28 of 2010.
5. The appellant took a ground of bona fide need as it
was required for establishing a medical clinic for his son,
who is a neurosurgeon. Upon consideration of the pleadings
and evidence on record, the Prescribed Authority recorded a
finding in favour of the appellant on the question of bona
fide requirement and passed an order of eviction dated
12.12.2012. The appeal preferred by the respondent-tenant,
being Appeal No. 04 of 2013, came to be dismissed by the
Appellate Authority, thereby affirming the order passed by
the Prescribed Authority.
6. Aggrieved thereby, the respondent-tenant invoked the
supervisory jurisdiction of the High Court under Article
227 of the Constitution of India and the High Court has
allowed the petition in favour of the tenant-respondent.
7. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and
have perused the material placed on record.
8. In the present case, the appellant has acquired the
2

--- Page 214 ---
premises in the year 1984 and filed a civil suit in the
year 1986 and since then, the tenant has been enjoying the
property.  The son of the appellant who wanted to establish
his clinic being neurosurgeon, has not been able to do the
same as the premises in question has not been vacated for
the last 40 years.  
9. This Court has considered the statutory provision of
Section 21 of the Act, 1972 and the principles laid down by
this Court in Ravi Khandelwal vs. Taluka Stores2. Para 16 of
the aforesaid judgment reads as under:
“16. When we turn to the facts of the present
case, what stares us in the face is that while
the suit may have been defectively instituted
within five years of the tenancy, more than 38
years have now elapsed since the suit was
filed. We opine that this passage of time
beyond the period of five years would wash
away the initial impediment against the suit.
We cannot lose sight of the fact that we stare
at a factual scenario where the vagaries of
litigation have prolonged the suit proceedings
for a period of 38 years. The plea of the
respondent is that the appellant should be
asked to file a fresh suit – perhaps their
confidence stems from the fact that if the
tenant has already been able to prolong the
proceedings for 38 years, a similar scenario
would  again  follow.  We  are  not  able  to
countenance such an interpretation which would
defeat the very purpose of creating an initial
restriction on the filing of the suit. To say
that the landlord should now, once again,
2 . (2023) 7 SCC 720
3

--- Page 215 ---
restart the proceedings because the initial
period of five years had not elapsed, even as
now 38 years have elapsed, would be a travesty
of justice.”
10. In the said precedent, this Court held that where
litigation has dragged on for several decades (38 years in
that  case),  the  passage  of  time  washes  away  initial
technical  impediments,  and  prolonged  litigation  cannot
defeat the legitimate need of the landlord.
11. Applying the aforesaid principles, this Court is of
the considered opinion that the interests of justice would
be subserved by setting aside the impugned order of the
High Court and restoring the concurrent findings and orders
of eviction passed by the courts below.
12. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order passed
by the High Court is set aside, and the eviction order
passed by the Prescribed Authority and confirmed by the
Appellate Authority stands upheld.
13. The respondent-tenant shall hand over vacant and
peaceful possession of the suit premises to the appellant-
landlord within a period of thirty (30) days from today.
14. The  respondent-tenant  shall  clear  and  pay  all
outstanding arrears of rent as well as the current rent
due, if any, within the aforesaid period of thirty days. 
4

--- Page 216 ---
15. The appeal is allowed in the above terms.
16. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IA  Nos.55920/2026  and  55922/2026  in  Crl.A.  Diary
No.4102/2026  and  IA  Nos.126927/2026  and
126928/2026 in Crl.A. No.2346/2026:
1. Heard. Admit.
2. The appellants who came to be tried for the offence
punishable under Sections 341, 294(b), 302, 506(2) of the
Indian  Penal  Code,  1860  came  to  be  acquitted  vide
judgment  dated  02.03.2022  and  the  said  finding  of
acquittal  came  to  be  reversed  by  the  High  Court  on
25.10.2025 in Criminal Appeal (MD) No.334/2022. Hence,
these appeals.
2

--- Page 221 ---
3. The case of the prosecution was that on 25.02.2015
that about 08:15 to  09:15 hours at Thatchanallur area,
near Galaxy Hospital, Palayamkottai, Tirunelveli - District,
Tamil Nadu, the accused restrained Ponniah – the deceased
after dragging him out of his auto, abused him in filthy
language and murdered him by inflicting sickle injuries on
neck, head, chest and left hand causing his instantaneous
death and thereafter, fled from the scene. The trial court,
upon  appreciation  of  the  evidence  tendered  by  the
prosecution, by its judgment dated 02.03.2022, as noted
hereinabove, acquitted all the accused on the ground that
the eyewitnesses, namely, PW-1, PW-3 and PW-4, were
unreliable, being interested witnesses, and their presence
at the scene of occurrence as well as their version of the
incident were doubtful. The trial court also found material
contradictions  in  the  prosecution  case  regarding  the
manner  of  assault,  the  role  attributed  to  each  of  the
accused  and  the  sequence  of  events,  thereby  creating
serious  doubts  about  the  prosecution  case,  apart  from
other grounds assigned in its judgment.
3

--- Page 222 ---
4. The  complainant,  being  aggrieved  by  the  said
judgment of acquittal, filed an appeal before the Madurai
Bench of the Madras High Court and on re-appreciation of
the evidence, the High Court found that the testimonies of
PW-1, PW-3 and PW-4 were reliable eye-witnesses and held
that minor contradictions did not affect the core of the
prosecution case. It was also noticed by the High Court
under  the  impugned  judgment  that  the  weapons  were
recovered  based  on  the  disclosure  statement  of  the
accused  and  same  was  accepted  as  a  corroboratory
evidence  connecting  them  to  the  offence.  Hence,
appellants, came to be convicted and sentenced to life
imprisonment. In these appeals, prayer for grant of bail by
suspension of sentence is sought for.
5. As could be seen from the records, the High Court
reversed the detailed reasoning of acquittal.  However, it
would suffice to state at this stage that High Court has not
recorded  finding  as  to  how  the  trial  court’s  view  was
perverse and it is not a plausible view. In the process of re-
appreciation of evidence, the material inconsistency that
4

--- Page 223 ---
has been brought to the forefront by the learned Sessions
Judge which undermines the case of the prosecution has
not  been  re-appreciated  as  could  be  seen  from  the
impugned judgment. However, we make it clear at this
juncture itself that this view is for the limited purpose of
examining the prayer for suspension of sentence and grant
of bail only.
6. Apart from the aforesaid facts, it would also emerge
from the records that accused persons were on bail during
trial and only after being convicted by the appellate court,
they  have  surrendered  and  they  are  undergoing  the
sentence. There being no any untoward incident that has
occurred being attributable to appellants while the trial was
going on or in other words, the conditions of the bail having
not been violated, we are of the considered view that
appellants  are  entitled  for  suspension  of  sentence  and
accordingly, the sentence imposed in Criminal Appeal (MD)
No.334/2022 by the Madras High Court, Madurai Bench
vide its judgment dated 25.10.2025 stands suspended and
appellants are ordered to be released on bail on such terms
5

fit to impose. Accordingly, the applications are allowed.

                             O R D E R
Heard learned Senior Counsel/Counsel for the parties.
2. A report has been filed on behalf of the learned Court
Commissioner. We have also gone through the same and find
that there is absolutely lack of cohesion between the
various Government bodies/departments, be it the State or
the Central. We further find that the officers of the
concerned  States/departments  have  not  understood  the
seriousness of the matter and the manner in which they are
required to act in the present case. We are unable to give
any benefit of doubt to the officers, as this Court, by
now has been monitoring the issue since more than a year
and a half, at least, with all seriousness and every
matter  is  discussed  threadbare  during  the  Court
proceedings before any order is passed. Still we find a
total lackadaisical approach by the authorities in either
assisting the learned Court Commissioner, or acting in a
manner which indicates that they are serious with regard
to what they say before the Court and what they actually
implement on the ground. Matters from keeping the sites
4

--- Page 229 ---
SLP (C) NO.12213/2019
free of encroachments, the cleanliness thereof, status
report, details with regard to ownership/settlement and
the current position – all are not forthcoming and even
the  authorities  which  in  law  are  presumed  to  be  in
knowledge of it and who are supposed to keep record of the
same, are blissfully ignorant of such details.
3. Thus, in the aforesaid background, the Court was of
the opinion that now the time has come where drastic
action is required by passing strict orders. However, at
the  request  of  learned  Counsel  representing  the  said
organizations/Government, by way of last indulgence, the
Court refrains from passing any stringent orders, for the
present.
4. We feel that a senior Central Government officer has
to  be  now  made  in-charge  so  that  the  issue  can  be
coordinated among  the official  respondents/departments/
Government, by such officer. In view of the nature of the
proceeding, we deem it appropriate that the Ministry of
Culture, Government of India through its Secretary be
impleaded  as  respondent  no.14.  Let  Delhi  Tourism  and
Transport  Development  Corporation  (DTTDC)  be  also
impleaded as respondent no.15.

Department (CPWD); Managing Director, DTTDC, and Land and
Development Officer, Ministry of Urban Development,  shall
be personally present in the Court.

7. We make it clear that any other engagement of the

IA No. 263756/2025 - GRANT OF BAIL IN CRIMINAL
APPEAL NO.1554/2022 
The appellant/applicant stands convicted by
the Trial Court vide order dated 09.12.2014, for
the  offences  punishable  under  Sections  148,
302/149, 307/149 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
and Sections 3(2)(v) of the Scheduled Castes and

--- Page 245 ---
                                                         3
Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act,
1989 and was awarded death penalty.
However, on appeal the High Court was pleased
to convert the sentence of death penalty into life
imprisonment, vide order dated 18.12.2018.
We have heard the learned Senior counsel
appearing for the appellant/applicant, the learned
Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent-State
and  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
complainant.
Learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant/applicant while placing reliance upon
the documents to indicate the physical condition
of the applicant, submits that apart from the
period of incarceration already undergone by the
applicant, two more factors may be weighed in by
the Court, namely, the deteriorating health of the
appellant/applicant and his old age.
The application for suspension of sentence is
vehemently opposed by the learned Senior Counsel

3. Ms. Malvika Kapila, learned counsel appearing for the
Delhi Development Authority, placed before us the Record of

resolution has been arrived at.  The Record of Discussion
is to the following effect:
“Meeting held under the Chairmanship of Hon'ble
Lieutenant  Governor,  Government  of  Delhi,  on
Conversion  of  Leasehold  Industrial  Sheds  of
DSIIDC (including Multi-Storeyed Units at Kirti
Nagar Packaging Complex) to Freehold
A meeting was held under the Chairmanship of
Hon'ble LG, Delhi on 06.08.2026 to discuss the
long-pending  issue  of  conversion  of  DSIIDC-
allotted  industrial  Sheds,  including  multi-
1

--- Page 250 ---
storeyed units at Kirti Nagar Packaging Complex,
from  leasehold  to  freehold.  The  CS,  ACS
Industries,  GNCTD,  Vice-Chairman,  DDA,
Commissioner (Land Disposal), DDA, and MD, DSIIDC
were present. The issue was discussed in detail
and  a  presentation  was  made  by  MD.  DSIIDC,
covering  the  background  and  history  of  the
matter, as summarized below:
Presentation  by  MD,  DSIIDC-Background  of  the
Issue and DSIIDC proposal
MD, DSIIDC apprised the meeting of the background
and history of the matter as follows:
DDA  allotted  various  land  parcels  to  DSIIDC
during the 1970s and 1980s for construction of
industrial sheds under the Half a Million Job
Programme and the Self Financing Scheme (SFS).
840 industrial sheds were constructed under the
Half a Million Job Programme and 456 sheds under
the SFS. DSIIDC has since carried out lease
administration  functions  such  as  allotment,
transfer,  mutation,  execution  of  conveyance
deeds, auction of cancelled units and eviction
proceedings.
In 2005, GNCTD notified the Conversion Scheme for
Industrial Plots/Built-up Sheds with the approval
of Hon'ble LG. After enactment of the Delhi
Industrial Development, Operation and Maintenance
Act, 2010 (DIDOM Act, 2010), DSIIDC became the
nodal agency for operation, maintenance and lease
administration of notified industrial areas.
DSIIDC approved conversion of industrial sheds
under the Half a Million Job Programme and SFS on
10.02.2011, and in 2012 initiated conversion at
Kirti  Nagar  Packaging  Complex  and  Mangolpuri
Engineering Complex. However, during examination
of conversion of multi-storeyed industrial units,
it emerged that:
(i) the Conversion Scheme, 2005 contained no
methodology for multi-storeyed units;
(ii) lease deeds in respect of Kirti Nagar
land parcels had not been executed by DDA in
favour of DSIIDC; and
(iii)  several  policy  and  legal  issues
2

--- Page 251 ---
required clarification.
Meanwhile, the Allottees of Kirti Nagar Packaging
Complex filed writ petitions in 2018 (W.P.(C) Nos.
179/2018,  9220/2018,  9268/2018  and  9270/2018)
after  DSIIDC  rejected  their  conversion
applications  on  grounds  that  the  Conversion
Scheme, 2005 did not cover multi-storeyed units
along with the lease administration not being
transferred by DDA. The Hon'ble Single Judge
(22.05.2019) upheld DSIIDC's stand; the Hon'ble
Division Bench (29.03.2023) reversed this and
directed  DSIIDC  to  process  the  conversion
applications. DSIIDC thereafter filed SLP (Civil)
Diary No. 46550/2023 before the Hon'ble Supreme
Court, while DDA separately filed SLP (Civil)
Diary No. 13550/2025 after its Review Petition
was dismissed. As per the latest status, both
SLPs are listed before the Hon'ble Supreme Court
on 07.08.2026.
Keeping the impending court decision, DSIIDC has
put up two proposals, in the presentation,
(1) Transfer of lease administration from DDA
to  DSIIDC  and  simultaneously  evolved  a
methodology  for  determining  conversion
charges for multi-storeyed industrial units.
(2) The conversion process to be done by DDA
and DSIIDC will collect all its outstanding
dues  from  the  property  allottee  before
freehold conversion.
After  detailed  deliberations,  following  was
resolved:
1. Conveying Authority: DDA, as the lessor
and  title-holder,  shall  be  the  competent
authority  to  process  and  execute  the
conversion of the properties to freehold, and
shall be entitled to levy and recover the
applicable conversion charges/fee from the
allottees.
2.  Condition  Precedent-Clearance  of  Dues:
DSIIDC shall first ascertain and recover all
outstanding  dues  payable  to  it  by  the
respective property allottees. Issuance of a
No Objection Certificate (NOC) by DSIIDC in
favour of DDA, certifying clearance of such
3

--- Page 252 ---
dues,  shall  be  a  mandatory  condition
precedent  to  DDA's  processing  of  the
conversion in each case.
3. Inter-Agency Reconciliation: Any residual
legal or financial issues arising between DDA
and DSIIDC shall stand outside the scope of
this resolution and shall be reconciled and
settled internally between the two agencies,
without prejudice to the conversion process
for individual allottees.”
4. It has been agreed by the parties that the parties
shall abide by the resolution terms.
5. Accordingly, the Appeals stands disposed of in terms
of the Record of Discussion.  
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

Leave granted. 
2. The appellant, Secretary, Board of Basic Education, 
Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh, is aggrieved with the impugned 
order issued in the contempt case , prima facie finding 
disobedience with the judgment and order dated 26.09.2023 
passed in Writ Appeal No.6926 of 2023, in which the first 
respondent was the appellant. 
3. The impugned order indicates that the direction in the 
judgment from which contempt is alleged, was to consider 
the claim of the writ petitioner in terms of Rule 8(2)(d) of the 
U.P. Basic Education (Teachers)(Posting) Rules, 20 08. It was 
found that despite the rule having been quoted, the 

--- Page 256 ---
Page 2 of 4 
 
 
impugned order does not consider its impact; which gave 
rise to the notice issued on contempt.  
4. We are unable to find any contempt on a reading of 
the order passed at Annexure P6. Annexure P6 definitely 
quotes Rule 8(2)(d), which is to the effect that applications for 
inter-state transfer of women or male teachers, though, 
would not be entertained for 5 years, in special 
circumstances, applications of woman teachers would be 
considered for inter -district transfer to the district of their 
husband’s residence/ in-law’s place. It is also specified in the 
order that a Council Teacher has h er cadre in the local area 
(rural or city) and in the event of transfer, there is a change 
of cadre and none can seek transfer as a matter of right, 
especially, since at the time of appointment, the teacher had 
voluntarily chosen h er cadre and joined thereat. The order 
further looks at the provisions in the Right of Children to Free 
and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 1, which mandates a 
particular student -teacher ratio to be maintained in every 
school as specified in the schedule. 
5. Insofar as the petitioner is concerned, there are two 
grounds raised to reject her inter-district transfer request . 
One, that in considering the inter-district transfer on the basis 
 
1 Hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act of 2009’ 

--- Page 257 ---
Page 3 of 4 
 
 
of online verification done, the 1 st respondent received a 
weightage of 12 marks , while for being transferred out of 
Bahraich District on an inter -district transfer, the minimum 
cut-off weightage is 22. Further, it is also stated that in the 
Composite School, Sikanderpur, Development Block Mahsi, 
District Bahraich , where the 1 st respondent is posted , the 
student strength is 137 , against which only 2 teachers are 
working in the primary section. As per the Act of 2009, the 
school requires 5 teachers and if one of the two teachers 
available is transferred, it would disrupt the studies of the 
students enrolled. We are of the opinion that the reasons 
rejecting the transfer are fully justified. 
6. The plea of the 1st respondent in her application is that 
she is living with her two-and-a-half-year old daughter, alone 
in Bahraich, whereas her in-laws and her husband, who is the 
only son of his parents , are in Lucknow. This is a universal 
problem faced by employees and one cannot , on the mere 
displacement from the family, claim an inter-district transfer, 
which in the present case also entails a cadre change ; as a 
matter of right. Rule 8(2)(d) is only a relaxation insofar as 
woman employees are concerned , which cannot, however, 
result in jeopardizing the studies of the students. Every 
teacher should remember that the education al system is 

--- Page 258 ---
Page 4 of 4 
 
 
primarily for the students and not to further the career of the 
teachers or to enable convenient postings to the teachers.  
7. We find absolutely no reason to uphold the order of 
the High Court and we set aside the same.  
8. The Contempt Application (Civil) No.236 of 2024 shall 
stand closed. 
9. The appeal is allowed. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

appellants were original ly shown as witness es in the

respondent had purchased properties on 28.12.1998 from

2

3. FIR No.292/2025 was registered for the offences
punishable under Sections 189(2), 189(4), 191(2), 191(3),
190, 103(1), 118(1), 333, 351(3) of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 (“BNS”) against the appellant and eleven
others. A cross-FIR being FIR No.300/2025 resulted in
1

--- Page 281 ---
same Police Station registering for the offences punishable
under Sections 115(2), 118(1), 189(2), 191(2), 191(3), 296
and 352 of the BNS against twenty-one identified persons
from the rival faction. In FIR No.292/2025, chargesheet
has been filed and thirty-seven witnesses have been cited
as prosecution witnesses.
4. appellant asserts that injury found on the deceased
is attributed to him and at the highest, the injury caused
to one Mr. Samadhan Mohe is attributable to him which is
simple injury and as such he seeks for grant of bail.
5. It is the case of the prosecution that on 28.08.2025,
the complainant faction allegedly went to the spot after
receiving information that members of Solanke Faction
had entered their house and were assaulting persons
residing therein and it resulted in armed scuffle between
two groups and in the said fiasco, Rishikesh Subhash Mohe

Prajwal and Shrikant Mohe. Before the High Court, the
2

--- Page 282 ---

Samadhan Mohe and caused grievous fracture injuries.

entitled for the similar relief. Hence, we allow this appeal,

1

--- Page 286 ---
at  Dongripali  Police  Station  in  the  District  of
Sarangarh-Bilaigarh (Chhattisgarh) under Section 20(B) of

(for short, ‘NDPS Act’).
5. Prosecution case is that on 31.01.2025, acting on a
confidential information, police  intercepted a pick-up
vehicle wherefrom 89.320 kgs of Ganja were recovered.
Based on the statement of the co-accused, appellants were
arrested on 09.11.2024 and have been in custody since
then.
6. Learned counsel for the appellants submits that there
are serious irregularities in the sampling of contraband
and sending them for chemical examination. Further, he
submits that as on today, appellants are in custody for
more than one year and 11 months. Prosecution has cited
15 prosecution witnesses in the trial out of which
evidence of only 8 witnesses have been recorded so far.
Early conclusion of the trial does not appear to be a
reasonable possibility. He also submits that there are no
criminal antecedents against the appellants. Therefore,
appellants may be enlarged on bail.
7. Learned State counsel on the other hand submits that
considering the quantum of the contraband seized which is
beyond the commercial quantity, it would not be prudent
to enlarge the appellants on bail at this stage.
8. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and on
due consideration, we are of the view that appellants may

detention undergone by them.

jurisdictional Special Court, within a maximum period of
7 days from today, whereafter they shall be enlarged on
bail on such terms and conditions as may be deemed
appropriate.

of.

petitioner.
3. It is the case of the prosecution that on the fateful
day and date of incident, the petitioner assaulted his wife
and due to the injuries suffered, she ultimately succumbed
and died. The injuries noted in the post-mortem report are
as under:-
“Internal Examination: The internal examination of the
dead body of the deceased Hemwati was conducted by me at
12:05 P.M. The body of the deceased was of normal build.
There was swelling near the right eye.
1. There was a fracture in the skull, cranium
and vertebrae (temporal bone) of the deceased.
2. The membranes of the brain of the deceased
were ruptured and blood had collected in it.
3. Blood had collected in the brain and spinal
cord of the deceased.
4. The diaphragm, ribs, soft tissues, lungs,
throat and trachea of the deceased were congested.
5. The right lung and left lung of the deceased
were congested and intact.
6. The left side of the heart of the deceased
was empty and blood had collected in the right
side of the heart.
7. The  contents  inside  the  stomach  of  the
deceased were congested and intact.
8. The  membranes  of  the  intestines  in  the
abdomen of the deceased were congested.
9. There was a clot of blood in the mouth,
oesophagus and trachea of the deceased.”
2

--- Page 292 ---
4. In the course of the trial, the Trial Court examined

deceased succumbed to the injuries on 30.12.2021. It appears

assault, the PW-1 – father and PW-7 – sister of the deceased
visited the deceased at her matrimonial home. At that point
of time, the deceased is said to have made an oral dying
declaration  that  she  was  mercilessly  assaulted  by  her
husband, i.e., the petitioner before us on some petty
domestic issues.
6. On 30.12.2021, the family members again visited the
deceased  as  her  condition  worsened.  They  visited  the
deceased on 30.12.2021 at the instance of the call made by
the petitioner-accused.  Ultimately, she died. She breathed
her last on 30.12.2021.
7. The FIR was registered on 02.01.2022 by the father of
the deceased, i.e., PW-1, however, on 31.12.2021, case was
registered by the Police and an inquiry was initiated under
Section 174 of the Cr.P.C. for unnatural death.
8. At the end of the investigation, the Investigating
Officer filed charge-sheet against the petitioner for the
3

--- Page 293 ---
offence of murder.
9. The Trial Court held the petitioner guilty of the
alleged offence of murder and sentenced him to undergo life
imprisonment with fine.
10. The petitioner went in appeal before the High Court.
The High Court, by a very cryptic and in a very casual
manner discussed the evidence of PW-1, PW-2, PW-3, PW-4, PW-
11 and ignored the most important evidence of PW-7 – sister
of the deceased.
11. Shockingly, the High Court thought fit to partly allow
the appeal by altering the conviction from Section 302 to
Section 304 Part II of the IPC. In the opinion of the High
Court, the case would fall within Exception 4 to Section 300
of the IPC.
12. Assuming for the moment that the High Court was of the
view that the case would fall within Exception 4 to Section
300, we fail to understand how the conviction could have
been under Section 304 Part II of the IPC. The conviction at
the most could have been under Section 304 Part I of the
IPC.
13. In any view of the matter, we are of the opinion that
there was no question for the High Court to bring the case
within Exception 4 to Section 300 of the IPC.
14. We are inclined to interfere with this part of the High
Court Judgment and call upon the accused to show cause as to
why the conviction imposed by the Trial Court for the
offence of murder should not be restored.

Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the parties.
3. The present  appeal is  directed against  the impugned
judgment and final order dated 15.10.2025 passed by the
Division Bench of the Gauhati High Court, Aizawl Bench in I.A.
(Civil)/52/2025 in W.A.No.5 of 2025, whereby the application
filed by the appellants seeking condonation of delay of 583
days in filing the writ appeal was dismissed.
4. The question for consideration is whether the High Court
was justified in refusing to condone the delay of 583 days in
filing the Writ Appeal. The High Court, in the impugned order
found that the delay had not been sufficiently explained by
the appellants. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant(s)

--- Page 296 ---
2
submits that the writ appeal involves substantial questions
relating to the liability to pay compensation under the
supplementary award and that the High Court ought to have
permitted the appellant to get the matter examined on its
merits.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent(s) submits
that the respondent(s) are poor villagers/landowners and have
been  awaiting  the  benefits  under  the  Award  for  nearly
seventeen years.
6. The fact remains that the proceedings before the learned
Single Judge had culminated in an order directing payment of
compensation, and the Division Bench, while considering the
application for condonation of delay, did not examine the
matter on merits and confined itself solely on the question of
delay in filing the writ appeal.
7. However, having regard to the nature of the dispute and
the fact that issues of fact and law arise for consideration
in the writ appeal, we are inclined to hold that the appellant
ought to have been afforded an opportunity of having the writ
appeal considered on its merits by the Division Bench.
8. At the same time, we are conscious of the fact that the
delay has not been satisfactorily explained and that the
respondents have been kept out of the benefits of the order

--- Page 297 ---
3
passed by the Single Judge, on account of the delay in filing
the writ appeal. In these circumstances, while condoning the
delay, it would be appropriate to impose costs upon the
appellant.
9. Accordingly,  the  impugned  judgment  and  order  dated
15.10.2025 passed by the High Court is set aside. The delay of
583 days in filing the writ appeal is condoned, subject to the
appellant paying a sum of Rs.10,000/-(Rupees Ten Thousand
only) to all the respondents, within a period of six weeks
from the date of receipt of a copy of this order.
10. The writ appeal shall stand restored to its original
number and be considered by the Division Bench of the High
Court on its own merits, in accordance with law.
11. The  appeal  stands  allowed  in  the  above  terms,
accordingly.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

recommendations emanating from the respondent-Departments.
For ease of reference, we extract the exact words of
our order as under:
“We also direct that the respondent-Departments to
reconsider the recommendations made by the Sabharwal
Committee in its Report in light of the fact that the
matter is now taken up by this Court in order to
ameliorate the conditions of the out boarded cadets and
we expect that certain favourable recommendations would
be emanating from the respondent-Department in this
3

--- Page 303 ---
regard.”
Learned ASG has drawn our attention to the affidavit
filed on 23.09.2026. Paragraph 10 of the said affidavit no
doubt reiterates what has been extracted above. It also
extracts certain recommendations of the Sabharwal Committee
made in its 2015 Report. However, there is no whisper in
the affidavit as to whether the Committee’s recommendations
were reconsidered by the respondent-Departments. All that
is stated in paragraph 14 is that a meeting was held by
DESW on the issues raised by the Services, under the
chairmanship of Secretary (ESW) on 22.08.2022 and the
proposal with regard to grant of disability pension to ex-
cadets boarded out was considered and the relevant decision
has been extracted.
It is clear as daylight that there has been no
reconsideration of the Sabharwal Committee’s report by the
respondent-Departments pursuant to our direction. We say
that there has been non-compliance of our direction issued
above on 04.08.2026.
Before we pass any other order which may be adverse
to the respondent-Departments, we give one more opportunity
to the respondent-Departments to comply with our aforesaid
direction and to place on record the minutes of the meeting
to be held pursuant to our direction on record. 
For  that  purpose,  we  adjourn  this  matter  to

witnesses have been examined before the Trial
Court. The appellant also does not have any
prior criminal antecedents.  The recovery of
the alleged contraband was made when he was
abroad.
Taking  note  of  the  aforesaid
circumstances, we are inclined to set aside
the impugned order and grant regular bail to
the appellant.
Accordingly, the impugned order stands
set  aside  and  the  appellant  is  granted
regular bail on such terms and conditions
subject  to  the  satisfaction  of  the  Trial
Court.
The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.

respondent-husband instituted the divorce petition in West
Bengal. It is submitted that the distance between the two
places is approximately 1,500 km, causing grave hardship and
inconvenience to the petitioner to contest the proceedings in
West Bengal.

1

prayer for transfer, contending that the respondent resides
in West Bengal, and as such, no case for transfer is made

case, this Court is of the opinion that the present transfer
petition deserves to be allowed.
5. Accordingly, we allow the transfer petition and direct
the transfer of MAT No. 1725 of 2025, titled as  “Soham
Dasgupta vs. Shivangi Choudhury” , pending before the court of
Additional  District  Judge,  5th Court,  Barasat,  North  24
Parganas, West Bengal to the Principal Judge, Family Court,
South-East District, Saket Courts, New Delhi.
6. Let the record of the case be transferred without delay.
7. A copy of this order be sent to the concerned court for
compliance. If video conferencing facility is available with
the transferee Court, the benefit of the same shall be
extended to the parties on such dates when their physical
appearance is not required. It is made clear that this Court
has not expressed any opinion on the merits of the matter.

2 PMAY
1

--- Page 356 ---
3. Rejection of an application for pre-arrest bail moved by the appellant

Calcutta, Circuit Bench at Jalpaiguri 4. Hearing the application for pre-
arrest bail5 on 19 th August, 2026, a Single Judge of the High Court
granted ad-interim protection to the appellant. Such protection came to
be extended twice on 21 st August, 2026 and 10 th September, 2026 by
orders of different Single Judges upon consideration of status reports
placed before the High Court acknowledging compliance of the orders
and co-operation by the appellant with the investigating agency.
4. Another Single Judge, however, by a final order dated 29 th September,
2026 rejected the application seeking pre-arrest anticipatory bail on the
ground  that  the  appellant  prima  facie  may  have  facilitated
embezzlement of public funds, which stands impugned before us. We
hasten to note that in the very order the High Court observed that the
appellant has been complying with the orders passed from time to time
and was also co-operating with the investigating agency.
5. Mr. Mehta, learned Solicitor General emphasizes that even lately,
members of the public who were otherwise not entitled but had
received financial benefits under PMAY were returning the same; hence,

--- Page 357 ---
6. Since the appellant has joined investigation since the first order was

by responding to the notices issued to him seeking production of bank
account details, and the fact that the FIR has been lodged after a
substantial delay from date of the alleged offence, we are of the
considered opinion that the High Court fell in error in not granting the
benefit of pre-arrest bail to the appellant.
7. In view of the above, the appeal succeeds. The impugned order is set
aside.

dissuade any person acquainted with the facts of the case from
disclosing such facts to any police officer or to the court.

terms and conditions imposed by it, the trial court shall be at liberty to
cancel the bail of the appellant.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026 
(@Special Leave to Appeal (Crl.) No(s).9963 of 2026) 
 
 
 
ROOP SINGH                                            
……Appellant(s) 
 
VERSUS 
 
STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ANR. 
                          ……Respondent(s) 
 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. Leave granted. 
2. A consensual relationship of about nine years has 
resulted in an allegation of rape when the appellant 
married another woman. 
3. The First Information Statement in the FIR annexed 
as Annexure P2 indicates that in the year 2011, the 
appellant got acquainted with the 2nd respondent, 
who was staying with her brother. There is a 
statement that the appellant proposed to her, and 
then they commenced a physical relationship. It is 
also alleged that the 2nd respondent; admittedly 
married at that time, broke her relationship with 
her own in-laws. Subsequently, the appellant married 
on 30.4.2021 and on the very next day FIR was 
lodged.  
4. The High Court, by an order in which various 
decisions of this court were referred to, found the 
FIR prima facie  revealing a cognizable offence; 
which we are unable to comprehend, as the consensual 
relationship for nine years is admitted by both 
parties. That the appellant expressed a desire to 

--- Page 371 ---
marry the 2nd respondent, and that a physical 
relationship was permitted, is also admitted; that 
the said relationship was commenced and continued 
when the 2nd respondent was married is also 
admitted. 
5. Even when the appellant and the 2nd respondent got 
acquainted, the 2nd respondent was married from 2006 
onwards. There is said to be a “social divorce ” 
obtained from a Panchayat in 2019, which in any 
event is not valid. The 2nd respondent is an 
educated woman; a postgraduate. The 2nd respondent, 
a married woman, entered into a consensual 
relationship with another  man, and when he got 
married, she took cudgels against the appellant, 
alleging enticement on promise to marry, which, in 
the facts and circumstances, we find unable to 
accept. 
6. FIR No.139 of 2021 lodged at Police Station Sapota, 
District Karauli, is hereby quashed; there shall be 
no further proceedings hereafter in pursuance to the

1

--- Page 375 ---
partnership firm M/s. Qayamuddin Khan & Co. had carried

cognizance, however, the trial has not yet commenced.

appeared before the Trial Court for which non-bailable
warrant of arrest has been issued. Even after the interim
protection was granted by this Court, he failed to appear
before the Trial Court.

Court was not being accepted by the Trial Court.

investigation is complete, and the matter is before the

--- Page 376 ---

anticipatory bail may not be warranted, however to avoid
any mis-construction of the provisions of law, we are of
the view that the interim protection granted by this
Court on 03.06.2026 should be made absolute.
11. It is ordered accordingly.
12. We also direct the appellant to appear before the
Trial Court on the next date fixed which we have been
informed is on 21.11.2026 and submit bail bond which
shall be accepted by the Trial Court.

4. Heard learned counsel appearing for the respective
parties and perused the material available on record.
5. Leave granted.
6. Learned counsel for the appellant has asserted that
the regular bail application of the appellant has been
decided and dismissed in the absence of the appellant’s
counsel before the High Court. He contends that because
of the non-appearance of counsel, the appellant went
unrepresented and, therefore, the case of the appellant
could not be projected effectively before the High Court.
He prays that the impugned order be set aside and the
matter be remanded to the High Court for a fresh decision
on the application.
1

--- Page 387 ---
7. A perusal of the impugned order dated 25.04.2026
clearly indicates that the appellant’s counsel before the
High Court was not present on the said date. However, the
High Court, instead of proceeding to decide the matter as
such, should have resorted to taking the assistance of a
legal aid counsel or an  amicus  curiae , to project the
stand of the appellant.
8. We, therefore, set aside the impugned order dated
25.04.2026 passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at
Bilaspur in MCRC No.2682/2026 and remand the case for a
fresh decision on merits.
9. The parties shall appear before the High Court on
29.10.2026.
10. Accordingly, the present appeal is allowed.

of.

                   Mrs.Bharti Tyagi, Adv.

For Respondent(s)  Mr. Shikhil Suri, Sr. Advocate (Amicus Curiae) 
    Mr. Vikas Singh Jangra, AoR (Amicus Curiae)
         Mr. Vibhor Choudhary, Adv. 
    Ms. Wamika Chadha, Adv.

--- Page 395 ---
2
          
                             O R D E R
Heard Mr. Vikramjit Banerjee, learned Additional Solicitor
General appearing for the petitioner-Union of India and Mr. Shikhil
Suri, learned Senior Counsel, who is also the learned Amicus Curiae
in the present cases.
2. The Court records its utter disappointment and displeasure at
the conduct of the officers of the Ministry of Railways in such a
serious matter concerning the safety of the common man. The
Railways  have  been  representing  before  this  Court  that  all
necessary steps are being taken in this regard. However, it appears
that such assurances have remained largely on paper and that no
substantial  change  has  taken  place  on  the  ground.  Even  the
budgetary provisions indicated for the targeted areas relating to
the safety of the common man and prevention of untoward incidents
have not been fully utilized.
3. In view of the aforesaid position, where there appears to be
hardly any progress on the ground, the Court is constrained to
direct the Chairman and Members of the Railway Board to remain
personally present before this Court on the next date of listing
i.e., 16.11.2026 at 03:00 p.m.
4. The Chairman and Members of the Railway Board shall be
personally held responsible, if the Court finds that assurances are
being given before this Court without there being corresponding
seriousness on the part of the Railways to ensure effective
implementation on the ground. The Court is particularly concerned
that despite budgetary provisions having been made, even basic

--- Page 396 ---
3
safety requirements appear not to have been adequately complied
with and that the provisions made have remained substantially
unimplemented. 
5. Coming to the issue of insurance coverage, at present, only
persons purchasing tickets online are provided the benefit of
insurance coverage upon payment of a nominal additional amount. The
Court has granted sufficient time to the authorities to devise a
mechanism for extending such coverage to persons belonging to the
lowest strata of society, who, in most cases, purchase their
tickets at the railway reservation counters while undertaking
journeys by train. As there has been no progress on this aspect
either, we direct that within two weeks, i.e., with effect from
27.10.2026, all tickets sold over the counter at all railway
stations shall also be covered by insurance in the same manner as
tickets  purchased  online.  The  aforesaid  direction  shall  be
implemented mandatorily, failing which the responsibility shall be
directly upon the Railway Board.
6. We make it clear that on the next date of listing, if the
Court finds that there has been no substantial progress on the
ground as compared to the position obtaining today, the Court may
have  to  consider  whether  the  Railway  Board,  as  presently
constituted, is fit to be permitted to continue in office.
7. On the next date of listing, the Chairman and Members of the
Railway Board shall remain present and be prepared to explain how,
in their planning and implementation, there has been a shortfall of
almost one-third every year in achieving the targets relating to
the  basic  safety  measure  of  fencing  the  railway  tracks.  No

--- Page 397 ---
4
exception shall be made in this regard. All concerned shall remain
personally present before the Court on the next date of listing and
no prayer for exemption shall be entertained. 
8. After the order was dictated, Mr. Vikramjit Banerjee, learned
ASG submitted that the Court may grant him one last indulgence to
enable him to file a categorical affidavit setting out the actual
work carried out on the ground during the last one year, explaining
the reasons for non-achievement of the prescribed targets, at least
in respect of fencing, which is a basic safety requirement, and
also indicating the manner in which the Railway Board proposes to
ensure that the targets indicated before this Court are achieved
under all circumstances.
9. Having regard to the aforesaid submission, the direction
requiring the Chairman and Members of the Railway Board to appear
physically before this Court on the next date of listing is kept in
abeyance for the present.
(SAPNA BISHT)                                  (ANJALI PANWAR)

1. Heard  Mr.  Mahfooz  A.  Nazki,  learned  counsel

learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State.
2. The  present  Special  Leave  Petition  calls  in
question the correctness of the order dated 8 th May, 2026
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in
Criminal Misc.Bail Application No.5126 of 2026. By the
said order, the High Court has dismissed the regular bail
application of the petitioner in connection with FIR/Case
Crime No.87 of 2024 dated 2 nd June, 2024registered at
Police Station, Biharigarh, District Saharanpur, Uttar
Pradesh for the offences punishable under Sections 8, 20
and 29 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances
Act, 1985.
3. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner
submits that out of 6 accused, the petitioner is Accused
No.6.  According to the learned counsel, admittedly, no
recovery has been made from the petitioner; he has been
implicated based on the statement of the co-accused and
he has already undergone 2 years and approximately 4
months in custody.  Learned counsel further submits that
the other four accused from whom the recoveries were
     
           SLP (Criminal) No.12155/2026 Page 2 of 4

--- Page 404 ---
effected are on bail.  Insofar as the antecedents are
concerned, learned counsel submits that even in that case
the petitioner is implicated on the confession of the co-
accused, the petitioner is on bail.
4. Learned counsel for the respondent-State vehemently
opposes the contention of the petitioner. Learned counsel
inviting attention to the chargesheet, submits that the
material exists against the petitioner.
5. Having  considered  the  overall  facts  and
circumstances,  the  period  of  incarceration  already
undergone; the fact that the accused from whose conscious
possession the contraband was recovered are on bail;
period of custody undergone by the petitioner;  that 8
more witnesses are yet to be examined; that the trial is
likely to take some time to conclude and keeping in mind
the  principles  enshrined  in  Article  21  of  the
Constitution of India as well as the twin conditions of
Section  37  of  the  Narcotic  Drugs  and  Psychotropic
Substances Act, 1985 , we direct that pending trial, the
petitioner shall be enlarged on bail subject to the
satisfaction of the Trial Court.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026 
[Arising out of SLP (C)  No.34372/2026] 
 
STATE OF U.P. & ANR.                           …APPELLANTS 
 
 
VERSUS 
 
 
YADU SUGAR LIMITED                            …RESPONDENT 
 
AND 
 
  
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026 
[Arising out of SLP (C)  No.             of 2026 
@ Dy. No. 59759 of 2026] 
 
 
 
DHAMPUR SUGAR MILLS LIMITED & ORS.          …APPELLANTS 
 
 
VERSUS 
 
 
STATE OF U.P. & ORS.                            …RESPONDENTS 
 
 
O R D E R 
 
 
 
1. Permission to file special leave petition1 is allowed. 
2. Leave granted. 
3. The facts requiring consideration are noted first. B oth the  appeals 
before us arise out of a common dispute relating to allocation of sugarcane 
under the Uttar Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) 
 
1 SLP (C) Dy. No. 59759 of 2026 

--- Page 439 ---
2 
 
Act, 1953 2. The common impugned order was made on a w rit petition3 
instituted by the first respondent in the lead appeal , which is a sugar mill 
under the Act. The grievance of the said first respondent, canvassed before 
the High Court of Allahabad, was that the second respondent, i.e., the Cane 
Commissioner under the Act, did not allocate the requisite quota of 100.8 
lakh quintals, resulting in the first respondent being closed down for the 
crushing season 2025 -26. The reason for non -allocation of the complete 
quota, as per the State of Uttar Pradesh, was delayed payments in previous 
years on the part of the first respondent to the farmers growing sugarcane 
in its assigned area.  The excess amount of sugarcane was reallocated to 
other mills, including the appellant in the connected appeal. The High Court, 
vide the impugned order  dated 7th September 2026 , allowed the writ 
petition while observing that the true cause for the delayed payment was 
non-allocation of the requisite amount of sugarcane, in the absence of any 
consideration for pilferage . The High Court reasoned that such non -
allocation had affected production and, thereby, caused delay in payments.  
A directive was also issued to the Cane Commissioner to provide 100.8 lakh 
quintals of sugarcane to the first respondent for the upcoming crushing 
season of 2026-27. Aggrieved by the impugned order, these appeals have 
been carried to this Court.  
4. The fulcrum of the dispute is the procedure prescribed by the 
Sugarcane Act, particularly Sections 14, 15, 16, and 17. The Sugarcane Act 
sets out a comprehensive procedure for determining the quantum of 
 
2 Sugarcane Act 
3 Writ-C No. 26307/2026 

--- Page 440 ---
3 
 
sugarcane to be allocated to each sugar mill, and it is the case of the 
appellants that the first respondent bypassed these provisions by directly 
approaching the High Court.  
5. During the course of arguments, it was pointed out on behalf of the 
appellants that in consonance with Section 16 of the Act read with Rule 22 
of the U.P. Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Rules, 1954, the 
statutory authority for determining the quantum of allocation of sugarcane 
for the upcoming crushing season of 2026/27 rests with the Cane 
Commissioner. The High Court’s exercise of these powers before the 
commencement of the upcoming season would amount to usurping the 
jurisdiction of the Cane Commissioner; thus, not only was the writ petition 
premature, but interference of the High Court  even before the Cane 
Commissioner made its order was wholly appropriate.  
6. Mr. Rohatgi, learned senior counsel for the first respondent , sought 
to sustain the impugned order by submitting that  the power conferred on 
the Cane Commissioner , not having been exercised  despite a substantial 
lapse of time, the High Court was perhaps left with no other option but to 
make the direction it ultimately did.  
7. However, having sensed that his submissions are not persuasive 
enough for sustaining the impugned order, Mr. Rohatgi agreed to disposal 
of these appeals in the manner proposed by the Court.  
8. The impugned order is set aside. While the writ petition instituted by 
the first respondent shall stand dismissed, the Cane Commissioner is 
directed to pass an appropriate order with regard to allocation of sugarcane 
to the first respondent, in accordance with law, within a period of a fortnight 

--- Page 441 ---
4 
 
from this date, uninfluenced by any of the observations made by this Court 
or the High Court. Once an order is passed  by the Cane Commissioner, in 
terms of this order, the parties shall be at liberty to work out their remedies 
also in accordance with law. 
9. The appeals are, accordingly, allowed in part. 
 
10. Connected applications, if any, shall stand closed.

VAISHNAVI S. UGADEKAR APPELLANT(S)
